Name: 500 Rummy
Conclusion: The card you need may be visible in the discard pile, buried under several cards you'd rather not take.
Core rules: Meld sets and suited runs or add to exposed melds. Cards played score for you; cards still held count against you. Build a total of 500 across hands.
Detailed rules: Deal seven each, or thirteen in an agreed two-player game. Draw one stock card or take a visible discard and every card above it; use the chosen discard in a meld that turn. Sets need three or four of a rank, runs at least three in one suit; an ace can be low or high but not wrap. Discard to finish. Score aces at 15, tens and face cards at 10, other cards at 5; highest score when someone reaches 500 wins.
Recommendation reasons: Digging down into the discards creates an unusual trade: gain the exact card you want now, but risk holding several unwanted cards when someone goes out.

Name: 6 nimmt!
Conclusion: A card that looked safe can become the sixth card in a row after everyone else reveals theirs.
Core rules: Choose a card secretly and reveal together. Play the cards in ascending order onto four rows. If yours would be sixth, take the first five as penalties. The player with the fewest bullheads wins.
Detailed rules: Deal ten cards per player and start four rows. A card goes after the closest lower row end; only if it is lower than every row end may you choose which row to take. When you take a row, your card becomes its new first card. Count printed bullheads rather than the number of captured cards. After ten plays, score the hand and deal again. End after a hand in which anyone reaches at least 66 penalty points.
Recommendation reasons: Eight strikes a good balance: plenty can go wrong on the reveal, yet nobody waits long. The rules are quick to teach and the deck travels easily.

Name: 7 Wonders
Conclusion: A card you pass may come back as the workshop, trading post or military advantage that changes what your neighbour can do.
Core rules: Build a city over three ages. Everyone selects one card at the same time, uses it to build a structure or wonder stage or discards it for coins, then passes the remaining hand. Compare military strength with neighbours and finish with the most points.
Detailed rules: Each age starts with seven cards; play six and discard the last. Passing direction reverses in the second age. Buildings may require resources or money; an appropriate earlier building can allow free construction. You may buy eligible resources from neighbours, who still use their own production. Build wonder stages in order. Resolve military conflicts at the end of each age; after the third, score your city, sciences, guilds, wonder, treasury and conflict tokens.
Recommendation reasons: Even with a large group everyone chooses at once. A neighbour’s resources and military strength give you reasons to change which card you keep.

Name: 7 Wonders Duel
Conclusion: The card you take is also the card you uncover for your rival. One purchase can open a route to victory on the other side of the table.
Core rules: Take an uncovered card from the age layout to build it, sell it or build a wonder. Military and scientific supremacy win immediately; otherwise the higher civilian score after three ages wins.
Detailed rules: Only cards with no others on top are available. Your resource symbols can be reused; missing resources cost money, and matching production in the opposing city can raise the price. Two identical scientific symbols earn a progress token, while six different symbols win outright. Advancing the conflict pawn into the enemy capital also ends play immediately. Only seven wonders can be built between both cities. If neither side wins early, tally buildings, wonders, coins and other scoring effects.
Recommendation reasons: A good duel for players who like several threats at once. The struggle over a shared display makes choosing a card as strategic as building the civilisation itself.

Name: A Feast for Odin
Conclusion: A green tile might earn income or cover a penalty, but its awkward shape can leave a hole you spend the next round trying to fill.
Core rules: Send Vikings to action spaces to hunt, trade, build ships and explore. Tile goods onto your home board and islands, feed the clan at each feast, and finish with the most points after subtracting uncovered penalties.
Detailed rules: In the standard game, play seven rounds. Each action column requires a different number of Vikings, and an occupied space is unavailable. On the home board, green goods may touch diagonally but not edge to edge; blue goods may touch. Cover income numbers in order, collecting the lowest visible amount. Food set aside for the feast cannot also fill a hole in your home. In solo play, alternate two colours of workers so last round’s choices still block spaces.
Recommendation reasons: It works especially well for two: a blocked action usually has an alternative, and your partner’s turn gives you time to solve your own tile puzzle.

Name: Agricola
Conclusion: Another family member means another action every round and another mouth at harvest. Growth feels valuable precisely because it is not free.
Core rules: Place family members on action spaces to grow crops, raise animals, enlarge the house and develop occupations. Fourteen rounds include six harvests. Score the completed farm across several categories.
Detailed rules: A family member normally blocks its space for the rest of the round. During harvest, take one crop from each sown field, feed the family, then breed animals. In multiplayer, each person needs two food; a newborn who has not acted needs one. Each missing food earns a begging token worth minus three. A pair of animals of one type produces at most one offspring that harvest and needs room to house it. Solo feeding uses different requirements.
Recommendation reasons: A good three-player table for watching occupations and improvements gradually work together. A farm that felt unforgiving on a first play can become much more satisfying on a return visit.

Name: Alphabet Categories
Conclusion: The category stays the same, but the next letter can turn an easy turn into a genuine scramble.
Core rules: Name items in one category while advancing through the alphabet from A to Z. Answer within the agreed limit and avoid repeats; the fewest penalties after three rounds wins.
Detailed rules: Choose a broad category, such as foods or cities, and allow five seconds each. An incorrect or late answer gives a penalty; the next player tries the same letter. After two consecutive misses, skip that letter. End at Z or ten minutes, then reset with a new category. Ignore leading articles when judging initials.
Recommendation reasons: It gives a carload or waiting group a word game everyone can follow. Changing categories lets the same rules suit different ages and interests.

Name: Arkham Horror: The Card Game
Conclusion: Every lead costs time, and the investigation does not wait until you feel ready. Even an imperfect ending can become part of your campaign.
Core rules: Choose investigators and play through a scenario together. Collect clues to advance the act while the agenda and encounter cards push the threat forward. The scenario determines the resolution and what carries into the campaign.
Detailed rules: Each investigator normally takes three actions per investigation phase and may repeat actions such as moving, investigating or fighting. A ready enemy engaged with you can make an attack of opportunity when you perform many ordinary actions. For a skill test, commit cards with matching icons, draw a chaos token and apply modifiers. Meeting the difficulty normally succeeds; the automatic failure token overrides the total. Damage and horror have separate limits. This core set supports one to four investigators.
Recommendation reasons: Two investigators make a good pair: the story stays involving, waits are shorter than at a larger table, and someone can help untangle a particularly wordy card.

Name: Azul
Conclusion: A handful of blue tiles can finish the row you have been saving or spill onto the floor. You know exactly what the tiles are worth; the uncertainty is who will take them first.
Core rules: Take all tiles of one colour from a factory or the central pool and add them to one pattern line on your board. At the end of the round each completed line sends one tile to its matching wall space, scoring for the tiles it touches. When someone finishes a horizontal wall row, finish scoring that round; most points wins.
Detailed rules: Unchosen tiles from a factory move to the centre. Each pattern line holds one colour, and its wall row must not already contain that colour; excess tiles go to the floor line for penalties. The first person to take from the centre also takes the starting marker onto their floor line. A wall tile scores one if isolated; otherwise count its contiguous horizontal and vertical lines, counting the new tile in both if it makes both. Add end bonuses for completed rows, columns and colour sets.
Recommendation reasons: The draft gives beginners one clear question—what colour do I need?—and gives returning players a second one: what will I leave in the centre for the next person? That makes the shared supply as interesting as your own wall.

Name: Battleship
Conclusion: A hit gives you a lead without telling you which way the ship runs.
Core rules: Hide a fleet on your own grid and alternate calling coordinates on your opponent's grid. Record hits and misses; first to hit every enemy ship cell wins.
Detailed rules: Draw separate fleet and tracking grids, each ten by ten. Place straight horizontal or vertical ships of lengths five, four, three, three and two, inside the grid without overlap; touching is allowed. Announce hit or miss for each shot and announce a sinking when the last cell of a ship is hit. Ships cannot move.
Recommendation reasons: It travels as two sheets of paper, and a first hit changes scattered searching into a small deduction puzzle about the next shot.

Name: Beat That!
Conclusion: A two and a six can be twenty-six or sixty-two. That little reversal is the whole point.
Core rules: Roll two dice and arrange the digits into the largest possible two-digit number. The highest number at the table earns a point each round.
Detailed rules: Take one roll each with no reroll, put the larger number in the tens place and compare results after everyone has played. Tied leaders each score. Rotate the starting player and play five rounds; tied overall leaders can roll a deciding round. For a harder game agree to use three digits in every round.
Recommendation reasons: Making a big number out of a modest roll is a concrete way to explore place value. It also takes almost no time to teach.

Name: Beggar-My-Neighbour
Conclusion: A face card changes a routine flip into a countdown: can the next player turn up a face card in time?
Core rules: Players turn cards from personal face-down stacks into a common pile. A jack, queen, king or ace gives the next player a limited number of flips to answer; failure awards the pile to the last player who set a challenge.
Detailed rules: Deal out the deck as evenly as possible. The allowance is one flip for a jack, two for a queen, three for a king and four for an ace. A fresh challenge card immediately switches the obligation to the following player. Otherwise the challenger puts the whole pile under their stack and leads again. A player who runs out leaves; the last player with cards wins.
Recommendation reasons: A pile that looked safely won can change hands on the very last flip. The four different allowances also give beginners a reason to notice the face cards.

Name: Betrayal at House on the Hill
Conclusion: The room you reveal changes both the house and the story you may eventually face. Your fellow explorers are useful allies, at least until the haunt tells everyone what they are actually trying to do.
Core rules: Choose an opening scenario and explore the house together, adding rooms as you pass through new doors. Items, events and omens change the explorers' prospects. When a haunt begins, the scenario and triggering omen identify the adventure and any traitor. Follow the new victory conditions rather than score points.
Detailed rules: Choose an explorer with four traits and move up to their Speed. When discovering a room, draw a tile for the correct floor and resolve its instructions and any card symbol. After drawing an omen, roll one die per omen found so far; five or more triggers the haunt in this edition, and the last omen triggers it automatically. Consult the relevant books privately where instructed. Allies may now have different goals or knowledge, and some haunts have no traitor. Use the haunt's special rules when they override ordinary movement, combat or victory.
Recommendation reasons: The exploration and the haunt reward different kinds of play. A group that enjoys discovering a story together gets a second surprise when a familiar room or item suddenly matters to one side's objective.

Name: Blackjack
Conclusion: The interesting moment is just before you ask for one more card: an ace can save an awkward hand, but a face card can end it.
Core rules: Try to finish closer to 21 than the dealer without going over. Each player decides when to stop; the dealer follows a fixed drawing rule. Use score tokens and rotate the dealer.
Detailed rules: Deal each player two open cards and the dealer one up and one down. Face cards count ten; an ace counts one or eleven. Choose hit or stand. The dealer reveals, draws below 17 and stands on every 17, including soft 17. A surviving hand beats a busted dealer; equal totals push. A two-card natural beats other 21s and earns two points instead of one. No splitting, doubling or insurance.
Recommendation reasons: Hit or stand is easy to teach, yet drawing on a marginal total still creates suspense. Rotating the dealer gives everyone a chance to play both sides.

Name: Blades & Rose
Conclusion: The table sees the cards that appeared, but not who put each one in. A single weapon among the offerings can change what everybody thought happened.
Core rules: The White Rose faction must protect the Rose and make enough sacrifices. The Blood Blades aim to kill the Rose or enough Buds. Secret contributions are shuffled, revealed together and resolved by their combination.
Detailed rules: Use the player-count chart for roles, weapons and Bud thresholds. Follow the initial night procedure for who recognises whom. Players may discuss a hand but may not show it as proof. Placing a crystal activates its effect when possible. Playing a faction card does not switch its owner’s allegiance. If all crystals are used without an earlier victory, finish the round and check the White Rose side’s hands: any unplayed Rose or Bud gives victory to Blood Blades; otherwise White Rose wins.
Recommendation reasons: At eight, actions carry more of the deduction than sustained speeches do. It suits a group that wants hidden identities without a long debate every round.

Name: Blood on the Clocktower
Conclusion: Death changes your voice in town rather than silencing it: you can still argue, and your one remaining vote may decide the game.
Core rules: A Storyteller secretly assigns characters and runs alternating nights and days. Good usually wins if the Demon dies; evil usually wins if only two non-Traveller players remain alive and the Demon lives. Character abilities can change those outcomes.
Detailed rules: At night the Storyteller wakes characters in order. By day players may talk privately or publicly and make claims freely. A living player may nominate once per day. An execution needs a vote count at least half the number of living players, rounded up, and a uniquely highest total; a tie for highest means no execution unless broken. Dead players normally lose their ability and cannot nominate, but may talk and have one vote left for the game. A five- or six-character game changes evil’s initial information. Add Travellers beyond fifteen character players. Include one Storyteller in the total headcount. Use a paper or digital grimoire to track roles, night order and votes.
Recommendation reasons: Nine or more around the table gives a script room to breathe. It rewards arranging a full group and finding a Storyteller who can keep the information and the town moving.

Name: Bomb Busters
Conclusion: A teammate's third wire might be your matching seven. You cannot see its number, but its place between the other wires may tell you more than anyone is allowed to say.
Core rules: Work together to cut matching wires before the detonator reaches its limit. Players see their own wires and keep them sorted; teammates see the backs. To attempt a paired cut, point to someone else's wire and name a value you can match. Cut all required non-red wires to defuse the bomb.
Detailed rules: A correct call reveals the other wire and one of your matching wires. A wrong ordinary guess advances the detonator and gives the team information about the indicated wire; hitting a red wire loses immediately. You may cut matching wires from your own stand if you hold every remaining copy of that value. Yellow wires are called by colour rather than their printed sorting numbers. The mission card defines the starting mix, available equipment and any exceptions to the usual rules.
Recommendation reasons: Sorted wires turn a partner's silence into usable information. Revealing one pair narrows down several other positions, and later missions change the puzzle without discarding the shared deduction that made the first one work.

Name: Brass: Birmingham
Conclusion: An opponent can turn your coal mine into income by taking its last cube. The same rail link can open a valuable market for both of you. Few decisions on this map belong to only one player.
Core rules: Develop industries and transport links across a shared region over a canal era and a rail era. Spend cards to build, network, develop obsolete tiles away, sell goods, borrow money or scout for flexible cards. Score flipped industries and links at the end of each era. Highest total wins.
Detailed rules: Normally take two actions, paying a hand card for each; the opening round gives only one. Build with a matching location or industry card under its placement restrictions. Coal must travel through connected links; iron requires no transport connection. Selling eligible goods requires connection to the right merchant and usually beer. A mine or ironworks flips when emptied; sale industries flip when sold. Spending less moves you earlier in the next round. After canal scoring, remove canals and level-one industries before laying railways.
Recommendation reasons: Competition does not mean blocking every rival. If their sale uses your beer, or their new line helps empty your mine, you may both benefit. That tension makes the economic rules matter to the players watching someone else's turn.

Name: Bulls and Cows
Conclusion: Two numbers of feedback are all you get, yet every guess can rule out whole families of possible codes.
Core rules: Guess a secret four-digit code. Bulls are correct digits in correct places; cows are correct digits in other places. Find all four bulls before your opponent, or first in a group race.
Detailed rules: Use four distinct digits and a nonzero first digit for secrets and guesses. In a duel both players set codes and exchange guesses by rounds. Count each digit at most once; four bulls in the same round is a tie. With three or more people, rotate one code setter and have the others guess simultaneously, with truthful individual feedback.
Recommendation reasons: The feedback is sparse enough to invite careful deductions, but each new trial quickly tells you whether your theory was useful.

Name: Bunco
Conclusion: Everyone is watching for the same target, so even a spectator can spot a Bunco the instant it lands.
Core rules: Across six rounds, roll three dice for the current target, from ones through sixes. This individual version adds each player's round scores; highest total wins.
Detailed rules: One target face scores one per matching die; three target faces score 21 and end the turn. Three equal non-target faces score five. Keep rolling on any other scoring throw and pass on zero. As soon as one player reaches 21 in the round, record everyone's round total and advance to the next target. Add all six totals at the end.
Recommendation reasons: This individual-scoring version changes the target number each round. Players can chat between rolls and still notice when someone lands three of the target number.

Name: Camel Up
Conclusion: A trailing camel can carry the leader backwards. You are betting on a pile of animals, not five independent runners.
Core rules: Bet on a leg or the overall race, place a spectator tile, or roll a die to move a camel. A moving camel carries those on top of it; the highest camel in a stack leads. Most money at the end wins.
Detailed rules: A leg ends when five dice have been rolled; a racing camel crossing the finish ends the race immediately. The two crazy camels travel backwards and cannot win, but can carry racers. A spectator tile can push a stack forward or backward. Settle leg bets first, then reveal overall winner and loser bets in the order placed: early correct bets pay more. The second edition also offers betting partnerships with six or more players.
Recommendation reasons: At seven, the player working out the odds and the one betting on instinct both have something to cheer for. It suits a mixed table without asking everyone to approach the race the same way.

Name: Captain Sonar
Conclusion: Someone must listen to the enemy captain while everyone else keeps your submarine moving. A missed direction can matter more than a missed shot.
Core rules: Two teams command hidden submarines. Navigate, charge systems, manage breakdowns and track enemy orders to find a firing position. Inflict four damage to sink the enemy submarine.
Detailed rules: At eight, each boat has a captain, first mate, engineer and radio operator. Each reported move advances the crew’s tasks. A captain cannot cross an island or revisit the boat’s current underwater trail. The operator fits enemy directions to the map; weapons and detection systems depend on charge and working equipment. Surfacing allows repairs and clears the route but reveals the sector. Two or three players must play turn by turn; groups of four or more may choose real time.
Recommendation reasons: At four against four, everyone has a distinct job and a shared target. The pleasure is in the two crews trying to outguess each other while keeping their own boat operational.

Name: Carcassonne
Conclusion: Everyone builds the same countryside. A tile that gives your neighbour a useful road can also give you a way into a city you could never have finished alone.
Core rules: Draw and place one landscape tile with matching edges. You may place one of your limited followers on an unoccupied feature of that new tile. Completed roads, cities and monasteries score for the player or players with the most followers on them. When the tiles run out, score the unfinished features; highest total wins.
Detailed rules: A connected feature cannot receive a second follower directly, but formerly separate roads or cities can join. A tie for most followers gives each tied player the full score. A finished road scores one per tile; a finished city scores two per tile and per shield. A monastery surrounded by eight tiles scores nine. Return followers after scoring a completed feature. If using farmers, they stay in their fields until final scoring and count completed neighbouring cities.
Recommendation reasons: The follower supply gives each tile a second decision. A short road can pay now and return your piece, while a city offers more points only if the right edges turn up. The joint map keeps everyone interested in the next draw.

Name: Cartographers
Conclusion: The same forest can become a tidy border on your map and the missing piece of a village on someone else's. You discover how differently everyone read the same draw when you compare maps.
Core rules: Reveal exploration cards and have everyone draw an allowed shape and terrain on their own map. Four edicts set the scoring goals, with a different pair scored each season. Score your map after each of the four seasons; the highest cumulative score wins, or compare with the solo rating.
Detailed rules: Rotate or reflect a shape to fit empty spaces without covering occupied squares; most placements need not connect to earlier ones. A ruins card constrains the next shape, and an ambush sends your sheet to a neighbour to draw monsters. End a season once revealed time values reach its limit. Score the two edicts and all coins earned so far; subtract one per empty square orthogonally adjacent to a monster, even if it touches two. Solo ambush cards specify where to place their shapes.
Recommendation reasons: Seasonal scoring gives the map a changing purpose: an awkward shape now can prepare a much better score next season. Simultaneous drawing keeps the spatial puzzle intact whether you play alone or compare solutions with friends.

Name: Cascadia
Conclusion: A forest tile could finally join two parts of your landscape, but the elk paired with it may be exactly the animal you have nowhere to put.
Core rules: Choose one habitat tile and its paired wildlife token. Add the tile to your landscape and place the animal where its species is allowed. Score wildlife patterns and connected terrain after twenty turns; the highest score wins.
Detailed rules: A new tile must touch an existing tile; its terrain edges need not match. An animal may occupy any empty matching habitat, including an older tile. Filling a keystone tile earns a nature token. Spend one to choose a tile and animal from different pairs or refresh some or all of the wildlife display. Each species scores its card’s pattern. Score your largest connected area of each terrain, then habitat bonuses and unused nature tokens. Solo play removes one unchosen pair each turn.
Recommendation reasons: Choosing a single tile-and-token pair asks two different questions: how will the habitat connect, and where can the animal score? The solo game keeps both decisions.

Name: The Castles of Burgundy
Conclusion: One tile completes a region, another grants a fresh action, and a poor die roll may still be exactly what a worker can fix.
Core rules: Use two dice each round to take or place tiles, sell goods or gain workers. Expand a connected estate over five phases; score for completed regions, tile effects and remaining assets.
Detailed rules: Each phase lasts five rounds. A tile taken from a matching depot goes into storage first; placing it normally takes a separate die whose value matches an adjacent space of the correct colour. Spend a worker to raise or lower a die by one, wrapping between one and six. Once per turn you may buy a black-depot tile for two silver without spending a die. Larger completed regions score more, and finishing them earlier improves the bonus.
Recommendation reasons: Two dice can set off a satisfying sequence of tile effects. Four players get a familiar game worth revisiting when nobody wants another long rules explanation.

Name: CATAN
Conclusion: A settlement on a good wheat hex may give you plenty to bargain with, but it does not guarantee a single brick. The people around the map are a second way to get what the island will not give you.
Core rules: Build roads, settlements and cities on a shared island. Two dice determine which terrain produces resources for adjacent buildings. On your turn, trade resources and spend them to build or buy development cards. The first player to have ten victory points on their own turn wins.
Detailed rules: Everyone places two starting settlements with roads, reversing the order for the second placement. A producing hex gives one resource per settlement or two per city unless blocked by the robber. A seven produces nothing: anyone holding more than seven resource cards discards half, rounded down, then the roller moves the robber and may steal a random resource from an adjacent opponent. New settlements need an empty intersection at least two edges from the nearest settlement or city. Roads, harbours, knights and development cards offer different routes to ten.
Recommendation reasons: You can trade from a weak position if you have the one resource another player needs. That gives the table something to negotiate beyond dice luck, and makes your choice of trading partner matter as much as the exchange rate.

Name: Categories
Conclusion: The obvious answer may be perfectly correct and still worth nothing if someone else wrote it too.
Core rules: Write words for several categories using the same starting letter before time expires. A valid answer earns one point only if nobody else wrote it.
Detailed rules: Pick five familiar categories and one random letter, then set two minutes. Write privately; ignore leading articles and use the specified starting letter. Compare answers category by category: duplicates, blanks and invalid entries score zero. Vote on disputed answers, change the letter each round and total five rounds.
Recommendation reasons: Originality has a real payoff. Comparing what different people came up with under the same letter often proves as entertaining as writing the list.

Name: Challengers!
Conclusion: You coach the deck before the match, then watch its cards play out. One extra copy can save a bench slot and change the result.
Core rules: Improve your deck, then face your scheduled opponent in a flag match. After seven rounds, the two players with the most fans enter the final; winning that match wins the tournament.
Detailed rules: In an attack, reveal cards until their combined power meets or exceeds the power of the opposing flag holder. If you cannot do so before running out of cards, lose the match. When you lose the flag, put its defender and the cards under it on your six-seat bench. Identical names can share a seat; needing another empty seat when all are full also loses. A lost match does not eliminate you from the tournament. Solo and two-player games use different schedules.
Recommendation reasons: Eight players can all be in a match at once. The hands-off battles give a tabletop tournament the feel of an auto-battler.

Name: Charades
Conclusion: A familiar phrase becomes surprisingly hard to explain the moment you lose the right to speak.
Core rules: One player silently acts out a secret prompt and teammates guess aloud against a timer. Alternate teams and score one point per correct prompt.
Detailed rules: Prepare folded slips of accessible titles, activities or phrases and set a one-minute timer. Draw one slip without showing teammates. Mime without speaking, mouthing or spelling; guesses are unlimited. Discard the prompt whether solved or not, rotate actors and give both teams equal turns. Higher total wins.
Recommendation reasons: A gesture that seems obvious to the actor can send the team guessing in an entirely different direction. Playing off those guesses is the fun, and no special kit is needed.

Name: Chase the Ace
Conclusion: A single low card is dangerous, and the only person who might take it sits right beside you.
Core rules: Each player gets one card and one chance to keep it or exchange it with the next player. At the reveal, everyone tied for lowest loses a life; the last survivor wins.
Detailed rules: Start with three lives apiece and deal one card each. Beginning left of the dealer, either stand or offer to swap; the neighbor must accept unless they show a king. The dealer may exchange with the top of the stock. An ace is lowest and a king highest. Reveal together, remove a life from every lowest card, move the deal clockwise and repeat.
Recommendation reasons: One decision is enough to put the whole table on edge. Swapping away a poor card feels great until a neighbor turns over an even worse one.

Name: Cheat
Conclusion: A perfectly honest play looks just like a lie until someone risks picking up the pile.
Core rules: Play face down and announce the required rank, truthfully or not. A successful challenge gives the pile to the liar; a false accusation gives it to the challenger. Empty your hand to win.
Detailed rules: Deal the whole deck. Claims advance clockwise from aces to kings, then repeat. Play one to four cards for a claim. Before the next turn, any opponent may challenge; reveal only the most recent play. If even one card was wrong, its player takes the pile. A last play can still be challenged before the win is final.
Recommendation reasons: Every claim leaves you with a choice: challenge and make the bluffer take the pile, or risk being wrong and collecting it yourself. A confident delivery can make that decision harder.

Name: Chicago
Conclusion: Everyone wants a different sum each round, and a safe-looking seven feels nothing like a rare two or twelve.
Core rules: Play eleven rounds with target sums from two through twelve. Roll two dice up to three times to hit the current target and score one point. Most points wins.
Detailed rules: Take turns clockwise. Stop on the first hit; an early hit is worth the same as a third-try hit. On a miss reroll both dice, never holding one back. After everyone has attempted the same target, move to the next. Share a final tie or play a second match.
Recommendation reasons: Everyone chases the same total each round. Two dice can make a seven in more ways than a two, so changing the target changes the suspense.

Name: Chopsticks
Conclusion: Your fingers are the board, and an apparently dead hand can return if you redistribute your total well.
Core rules: Tap an opponent's live hand to add your hand's value to theirs modulo five, or redistribute your own finger total. A player with both hands at zero loses.
Detailed rules: Begin with one finger on each hand. Values range from zero to four. For example, a hand showing three hit by a two drops to zero, while four hit by two becomes one. A split must preserve the total, change at least one hand and keep both values between zero and four. Splits may revive a closed hand; turns alternate.
Recommendation reasons: It travels anywhere and makes small-number arithmetic part of a tactical choice. Only two hands are needed to try a different attack or rescue.

Name: Citadels
Conclusion: Knowing that the Assassin was available is not the same as knowing who took it. Every city plan comes with a guess about somebody else’s role.
Core rules: Secretly choose new roles each round. Called in rank order, characters collect resources, build districts and use their abilities. A completed city triggers the last round; highest city score wins.
Detailed rules: On a normal turn take two gold or draw two district cards and keep one. Pay the building cost and usually build at most one district with a name you do not already own. Roles can change these limits or interfere with others. In the five-player game described here, seven built districts complete a city; finish the whole round. Score district values and bonuses, including city completion and colour diversity. A tie goes to the higher-ranked role revealed in the final round.
Recommendation reasons: At five, the role selection gives everyone a plausible suspect. The fun is deciding whom to interfere with without letting a third player build unchecked.

Name: Clank! Catacombs
Conclusion: One more tile could reveal the treasure you want or leave you one turn too far from safety. The dragon does not wait for everyone to agree it is time to go.
Core rules: Play cards for movement, combat and buying power. Explore the catacombs, collect an artifact and survive the dragon. Noise enters the dragon bag and may return as damage; a qualifying thief wins on total treasure and points.
Detailed rules: Play your hand and use its resources to move, fight or acquire cards for future draws. Newly explored passages reveal tiles. When a dragon attack triggers, put accumulated Clank! cubes into the bag and draw cubes; your colour wounds you. Escape at the starting Crypt with an artifact to claim a 20-point mastery token. An artifact carrier knocked out in a safe area still scores; without an artifact or if knocked out in the Depths you score zero. Escaped players keep triggering dragon attacks.
Recommendation reasons: Three keeps the temptation to uncover another room without a long wait between turns. The next tile might be a reward or a nasty surprise.

Name: Codenames
Conclusion: A clever link between three words looks different when the next word over would make your team lose immediately.
Core rules: Divide into two teams. Each spymaster sees which words on the grid belong to which side and gives one word plus a number as a clue. Teammates guess agents; uncover all your agents first to win, but choosing the assassin loses immediately.
Detailed rules: Lay out 25 words in a five-by-five grid and hide the key from guessers. The starting team has nine agents, the other eight. A correct guess lets the team continue or stop; a neutral word or enemy agent ends its turn. Normally a team may guess at most the clue number plus one. Two or three people can use the small-group variants; four or more play the usual two-team game. A handwritten word grid, a matching secret key and coloured markers can substitute for the box.
Recommendation reasons: When a clue might fit two words, teammates have to decide which one their spymaster intended. A nearby assassin word can change the whole discussion.

Name: Colt Express
Conclusion: You can queue the perfect robbery and arrive to find that someone has punched you into the next carriage.
Core rules: Program actions for five rounds, then resolve the cards in the order played. Bandits move, steal, shoot and punch across the train. Finish with the most loot, including any gunslinger bonus.
Detailed rules: The round card sets the number and order of planning steps; tunnels may hide a played card. Instead of playing, draw three cards. Pick a legal target when your action resolves, not when you queue it. A shot puts a bullet in the victim’s deck, clogging future hands; the marshal sends a bandit to the roof with a neutral bullet. After round five, each bandit tied for most bullets fired earns $1,000. In the two-player game each person controls two bandits.
Recommendation reasons: Five bandits generate the kind of slapstick where everybody has a plan and nobody ends up holding the money they expected. It is an approachable introduction to programming games.

Name: Concentration
Conclusion: Every wrong guess still gives the whole table a useful piece of information.
Core rules: Turn over two cards from a face-down grid. Keep equal ranks and take another turn; otherwise turn both back in place. The player who collects the most pairs wins.
Detailed rules: Use two cards of each of the thirteen ranks. Shuffle the 26 cards into a regular grid without gaps. Show both cards long enough for everyone to see; never move unclaimed cards between turns. An unsuccessful turn passes clockwise. End when the last pair has been taken and count pairs, sharing a tie.
Recommendation reasons: Children and adults can play the same game with almost no teaching. Paying attention on someone else's turn can be more useful than making another guess yourself.

Name: Connect Four
Conclusion: A perfect square for a future four is useless if no piece yet supports it from underneath.
Core rules: Choose a column and place a mark in its lowest free cell. First to connect four marks horizontally, vertically or diagonally wins.
Detailed rules: Draw a board seven columns wide and six rows high. Pick different symbols and alternate one move at a time. Never leave an empty space beneath a mark or play in a full column. Check all directions after each move; stop on the first line of four. A full board without a line is a draw.
Recommendation reasons: Every piece must land in the lowest free space in its column. As well as blocking a row of three, you need to notice when your move will give an opponent the support for a diagonal.

Name: Contact
Conclusion: Two guessers are trying to think of the same word just before the one person who can stop them does.
Core rules: A word keeper reveals a prefix. Guessers try to connect on a different word starting with it; an unblocked match earns another letter. Guess the keeper's full word to win.
Detailed rules: Choose a common word of at least six letters and reveal its first letter. A guesser clues a different word with that prefix. Another signals contact; the keeper has about five seconds to block by naming the clue word. If not blocked, both guessers count down and speak together. Matching answers reveal the next letter, mismatches reveal nothing. A correct direct guess ends the round.
Recommendation reasons: It rewards the pleasure of a shared association, with an opponent racing to spot it too. Every extra letter makes the contest meaningfully different.

Name: Crazy Eights
Conclusion: An eight lets you turn a hand full of the wrong suit into a plan.
Core rules: Match the top discard by rank or suit, or play an eight to name a new suit. First to empty their hand wins.
Detailed rules: Deal seven cards each to two players, otherwise five. Turn one card face up, replacing it if it is an eight. If unable to play, draw one and play it immediately if legal; otherwise pass. Recycle discards except the top card when the stock runs out. For a longer match, score opponents’ remaining cards: eights 50, face cards 10, aces 1, others face value.
Recommendation reasons: Matching a rank or a suit gives new players a clear choice; an eight lets them change the suit. Anyone familiar with UNO will recognise the idea, and an ordinary deck will do.

Name: The Crew: Mission Deep Sea
Conclusion: Sometimes the winning play is to lose a trick on purpose, because the only person allowed to take it is sitting across the table.
Core rules: The crew share a mission made up of card-play tasks. Follow the led suit when possible; the highest trump, or highest card of the led suit if no trump is played, wins the trick. Complete every task together without openly discussing your hands.
Detailed rules: Deal the coloured cards and four submarine trumps. The highest submarine makes its holder captain and opening leader. Assign mission tasks: some specify who must win a card, others how many tricks someone must take or avoid. Unless the mission restricts it, each player may once reveal a non-trump card and mark it as the highest, lowest or only card of its colour in their hand. A failed task means a failed mission. At two, the captain plays an additional partly visible hand.
Recommendation reasons: Winning the trick is not enough: the right teammate has to win it. One carefully chosen hint can make a previously failed mission achievable.

Name: Cthulhu: Death May Die
Conclusion: Losing sanity can make an investigator stronger before it destroys them. The most memorable turn may come just when the group seems beaten.
Core rules: Combine an episode and an Elder One. Disrupt the ritual before attempting to damage the Elder One, then defeat all its stages before time or investigator losses defeat the group.
Detailed rules: Take three actions on an investigator’s turn, then resolve the Mythos and the location’s enemies or discovery. One stress rerolls one die just rolled; resting does not restore lost sanity. Before the Elder One is summoned, any investigator dying or going completely insane loses the game for everyone. After summoning, individual investigators can be eliminated, but losing all of them or reaching the end of the Elder One’s track still loses. A solo player controls two investigators.
Recommendation reasons: Pick it for a group that enjoys dramatic comebacks: a character near collapse can still help bring down a seemingly unbeatable enemy.

Name: Deception: Murder in Hong Kong
Conclusion: The one person who saw the crime cannot simply tell you the answer. The murderer, meanwhile, is allowed to sound just as helpful as any investigator.
Core rules: Each player other than the Forensic Scientist displays means and clue cards. The murderer secretly designates one of each from their own cards. The Scientist knows the pair and places markers on scene tiles to guide the investigators without speaking the solution. Investigators win by naming both cards correctly; the murderer wins if the investigation ends unsolved.
Detailed rules: The Scientist is a member of the investigating side, not a separate host. Initial tiles include cause of death, location and other aspects of the scene. Later rounds replace one ordinary scene tile to refine the clues. A player with a badge may spend it to accuse, naming the suspect's two cards. The Scientist only confirms success or failure, never which half was correct. A failed accuser may still discuss but has no second accusation. Larger groups can add an accomplice or witness with extra victory conditions.
Recommendation reasons: The Scientist's limited vocabulary is what makes the deduction interesting: “metal” can point toward several people's cards. In a group that likes talking through evidence, the murderer can steer that same ambiguity toward an innocent player.

Name: Detective: City of Angels
Conclusion: A witness can be telling the truth and still sound absurd. Deciding when to challenge the answer is as important as finding the clue.
Core rules: In Classic mode, one player is the Chisel, who knows the case. The detectives compete individually to solve it before the deadline. The first correct solution wins; if nobody solves the case, the Chisel wins.
Detailed rules: Each detective normally has four actions per day to move, search or question suspects about evidence. The Chisel chooses from the responses written for that question. A detective can challenge an answer, risking leverage if wrong. To attempt an early solution, turn in a solve token before taking any actions that turn. A wrong early guess costs the token but does not remove the detective. Unsolved cases go to final guesses. Solo and fully cooperative play use the separate Sleuth casebook instead of a Chisel.
Recommendation reasons: Three works well as one Chisel against two rival detectives. Even after learning the solution, it can be fun to run the case and watch what the others make of an improbable but accurate lead.

Name: Dig Your Way Out
Conclusion: The best shovel in prison is only useful if you can get it back to your cell before someone takes it off you.
Core rules: Spend two actions per turn searching the prison, acquiring or making tools, dealing with inmates and digging in the cell block. The first prisoner to reach the required tunnel score escapes immediately.
Detailed rules: Start in the cell block with three search cards and a background. Some actions work anywhere; others require a specific room. Cigarettes pay for deals, and gang membership or wounds can affect your options. To dig, discard an appropriate tool in the cell block and score its tunnel value. The target is twelve points with two or three players, ten with four, and eight with five or six. Merely holding a tool earns no points.
Recommendation reasons: Five gives the direct confrontation room to develop. With only two actions each, taking an early lead can make you the person everyone else decides to stop.

Name: Dito! (JinxO)
Conclusion: The obvious answer may match the whole table. A less obvious one can be better if exactly one other person thinks of it too.
Core rules: Each round, everyone fills a private three-by-three grid with three answers apiece to three prompts. Players then take turns calling out words from their grids. Matches score; a match between just two people earns a bonus. The highest total after three rounds wins.
Detailed rules: Write each answer in any unused square without repeating one on your board. When a word is called, everyone who wrote it circles it; if just two people matched, both mark a star. A caller with no match crosses the word out. Once anyone has marked all nine squares, stop immediately. Each circle scores one point, each star two more (one extra in the three-player Dito! game), and a fully circled row or column earns its printed bonus. Clear the grid between rounds.
Recommendation reasons: There are two decisions to enjoy in the same thirty seconds: what someone else might write, and which square should get that guess. A shared answer is useful, but a word that connects you with just one other player can finish a valuable line.

Name: Dixit
Conclusion: An illustration can stand for a memory, a song or a private joke. The storyteller needs a clue that reaches someone else without making the picture obvious to everyone.
Core rules: The storyteller chooses an illustrated card and gives a clue. Everyone else contributes a picture that could fit it. Shuffle and reveal the cards; everyone except the storyteller votes secretly for the original. Find the original or attract votes to your decoy to score. When someone reaches 30 at turn end, the highest score wins.
Detailed rules: If at least one voter finds the original but not everyone does, the storyteller and each correct voter score three. If all or none find it, the storyteller scores zero and each other player scores two. A decoy earns its owner one extra point per vote on it; nobody may vote for their own card. Refill hands and rotate storyteller. In the three-player game, deal seven cards each; each non-storyteller submits two decoys but casts just one vote.
Recommendation reasons: Choosing a convincing decoy gives the listeners just as much to do as the storyteller. The scoring rewards clues with more than one plausible reading, so comparing how people interpreted the pictures is part of the play.

Name: Dominion
Conclusion: Buying better cards improves your future hands, right up to the moment you must buy victory cards that do almost nothing when drawn. Timing that switch is the heart of the game.
Core rules: Everyone starts with the same small deck. Each turn, play an action if desired, play treasures and buy a card into your discard pile, then discard the turn's cards and draw a new hand. When the Provinces or any three Supply piles are empty at turn end, the player with the most victory points in their deck wins.
Detailed rules: Use ten Kingdom piles plus the base Supply. Start with seven Coppers and three Estates; draw five cards. A turn normally has one action and one buy, though card text may grant more. Play action cards in order and resolve each fully. When you need to draw from an empty deck, shuffle your discards into a new deck; a trashed card is removed instead. If scores tie, the tied player who took fewer turns wins, otherwise they share the win.
Recommendation reasons: The ten Kingdom piles are visible from the start, so you can plan around a particular combination rather than hope to discover it in a random pack. Changing those piles changes what a good deck looks like.

Name: Doodle Dash
Conclusion: The fastest sketch only helps if somebody can recognise it. A few good lines can beat a beautiful unfinished drawing.
Core rules: One player guesses while everyone else draws the same word. Finishing early earns an earlier chance to show your picture. Correct guesses score for the guesser and the relevant artists; most points wins.
Detailed rules: The guesser chooses a word number without seeing the card. Draw without letters, numbers or spoken clues. The first finisher takes the token; the second finisher rolls until the stop symbol appears. The guesser tries the token holder’s picture first, then the roller’s. If neither works, reveal the remaining pictures together; a correct final guess scores for that entire last group. At three players there is no central token. Rotate guessers after every card. Paper, word slips, a die with a designated stop result and a finish marker can stand in for the boxed pieces.
Recommendation reasons: A hard stop keeps seven people from waiting for the most meticulous artist. The hurry is part of the joke, not a test of who draws best.

Name: Dots and Boxes
Conclusion: Leaving three sides of one square can hand over an entire chain, not just a single point.
Core rules: Draw one edge between adjacent dots. Complete a square to claim it and immediately play again. When all edges are drawn, whoever owns the most boxes wins.
Detailed rules: Start with a square dot grid, for example five by five dots. Draw horizontal or vertical edges only, never a diagonal, duplicate or skipped dot. Mark each completed box, including both if one stroke completes two. Keep taking extra turns while scoring. With four players, agree in advance on individual or paired scoring.
Recommendation reasons: One line can close a box and earn another turn. Once a long chain appears, giving a few boxes away to keep control can matter more than claiming the first one.

Name: Drop Dead
Conclusion: The handful of dice keeps shrinking, and a lone surviving die can still bring a surprisingly good turn.
Core rules: Roll five dice until none remain. Any roll with a two or five scores nothing and removes all twos and fives; a roll with neither scores the sum of all its dice.
Detailed rules: Continue with only the active dice and keep points from earlier safe rolls. You cannot stop and bank or save an individual die. Each person completes one entire turn, and the highest personal total wins. Share ties or give tied players another complete turn.
Recommendation reasons: All players can follow the dwindling dice without learning a strategy. The tension comes from seeing just how long one or two dice can survive.

Name: Dune: Imperium
Conclusion: A card can open an agent space now or buy a stronger card later. Improving the deck means deciding which half of a good card you can afford to forgo.
Core rules: Use cards to send agents to spaces or reveal your hand for purchases and combat strength. Factions and conflicts award victory points. If someone reaches ten or the conflict deck is empty, finish the round and score endgame effects.
Detailed rules: Each agent turn requires a card showing the destination icon. Resolve the space and the agent part of that card. Revealing instead uses the reveal effects of your remaining hand and ends your agent turns for the round. Newly recruited troops normally enter your garrison; only deployed troops count in a conflict. Resolve conflict rewards before recalling agents. One- and two-player games use House Hagal to occupy spaces or otherwise supply opposition.
Recommendation reasons: Buying cards and trimming weaker ones can turn a patchy opening hand into combinations that work together. Building that deck is satisfying even outside a winning game.

Name: Dune: Imperium – Uprising
Conclusion: In a six-player battle, an ally may need you to activate their troops more than you need a point for yourself.
Core rules: Use agents and a personal deck to gain influence, resources and conflict rewards. In the six-player game, two teams of three compete. Add teammates’ scores after endgame effects; the higher team total wins.
Detailed rules: A team has one commander and two allies. Play a card with a matching icon to send an agent to a space, or reveal the rest of your hand for persuasion and combat strength. After revealing, you cannot send more agents that round. Commanders have no troops of their own; the arrows at their spaces activate an ally. Reaching ten points or exhausting the conflict deck triggers the end. Teammates discuss plans openly. One to four use the regular game; there is no five-player configuration.
Recommendation reasons: Six players get a rare three-against-three strategy game where both sides hear the planning. Coordinating well is demanding, but it gives the group a reason to try the matchup again.

Name: Durak
Conclusion: Defend too cheaply and someone can add a matching rank; spend your best trump now and you may miss it later.
Core rules: Attack the next defender with cards they must beat one by one. A successful defender discards the attack; one who stops must take the whole table. After the stock runs out, the last player holding cards loses.
Detailed rules: Use the 36 cards from six to ace, deal six each and turn up the trump suit. Lowest trump attacks first. Defend with a higher card in suit or a trump; a trump requires a higher trump. Others can add ranks already on the table, up to six attacks and no more than the defender's initial hand size. Refill to six with the attacker first and defender last. A successful defender attacks next; otherwise their turn to attack is skipped.
Recommendation reasons: Taking a small attack on purpose can save a trump for later. If you cannot cover the attack, though, picking it up is no longer optional.

Name: Egyptian Ratscrew
Conclusion: A face-card challenge can reverse with one flip, and a double lets anybody claim the lot.
Core rules: Flip cards to a central pile. Face cards and aces force a response; consecutive equal ranks may be slapped. The last player with cards wins.
Detailed rules: Against J, Q, K or A, the next player has one, two, three or four flips respectively to find another face card or ace. Finding one transfers the challenge; failing gives the pile to its initiator. The first valid slap on a double takes the pile. A false slap costs a card under the pile. A player who runs out has one chance to slap the next double.
Recommendation reasons: The race to react first gives it a different energy from a purely luck-driven flipping game. It is best when everyone enjoys quick, physical play.

Name: Euchre
Conclusion: Calling trump turns five cards into a commitment for your team. Going alone raises the stakes without adding another hand to manage.
Core rules: Play five tricks with a chosen trump suit. The trump jack and same-colour jack are highest. The calling team must win at least three tricks.
Detailed rules: Use the 9 through ace of each suit, five cards per person. Turn up one card to offer its suit as trump; if all pass, offer the other suits, redealing after a second full pass. Follow suit if able, counting the same-colour jack as trump. Callers score one for three or four tricks, two for a sweep, or four for a lone sweep. Defenders get two for stopping them. Play to ten.
Recommendation reasons: Short hands and the option to play alone make it a sociable partnership game with quick, consequential decisions.

Name: Exploding Kittens
Conclusion: Sooner or later someone must take the top card. The joke becomes a tactical question when one player knows what that card is and everyone else has watched them choose not to draw it.
Core rules: Play any number of action cards, then end your turn by drawing one card unless an effect says otherwise. An Exploding Kitten eliminates you unless you play a Defuse. The last player still in the game wins.
Detailed rules: Deal each player one Defuse and seven other cards. Shuffle one fewer kitten than there are players into the draw pile. Return spare Defuses to the deck, but use only two spares at two or three players. A player who defuses a kitten secretly puts it anywhere in the pile without looking through the other cards, ending that turn. Skip ends one turn without a draw; Attack makes the next player take extra turns; See the Future previews the top three cards. A Nope can cancel another action, even a Nope, but cannot cancel a kitten or a Defuse.
Recommendation reasons: The funniest reversal also has a real decision behind it: the person who just saved themselves can put the kitten straight back on top or bury it. That makes watching how opponents spend skips and shuffles part of the game.

Name: Exquisite Corpse
Conclusion: Everyone contributes a perfectly reasonable word, yet the finished sentence can be wonderfully strange.
Core rules: Pass folded paper around, adding one unseen sentence part at a time. Unfold the finished sentences and read them aloud; no scoring is necessary.
Detailed rules: Divide each strip into six sections. Add, in order, an adjective, a person or noun, an adverb, an action verb, another adjective and an object. Fold to hide each contribution before passing left. After six passes, return the strip to its starter and read the assembled sentence, adding connecting words if needed.
Recommendation reasons: Nobody has to produce a clever sentence on their own. Hidden contributions create accidental combinations no one could have planned.

Name: Farkle
Conclusion: Setting aside an easy five keeps you alive, but leaves fewer dice for a more valuable combination.
Core rules: Roll six dice, set aside scoring dice from this roll, then bank or risk the rest. A roll with no score loses the entire unbanked turn; scoring all six lets you roll six again.
Detailed rules: Single ones score 100 and fives 50. Three ones score 1,000; other triples score face times 100. Each extra identical die doubles that triple score. A straight from one to six or three pairs scores 1,500. Combinations must occur in one roll and cannot reuse dice. Once someone banks 10,000, everyone else takes one last turn; high score wins.
Recommendation reasons: Do you bank the points or risk another roll with the dice you have left? If all six score, you can pick up the whole handful and try again.

Name: Fictionary
Conclusion: A plausible definition can beat the real one, even if its author had never heard the word before.
Core rules: A rotating reader mixes one true definition of an unfamiliar word with players' inventions. Vote for the true one; score both for finding it and for attracting votes to your own fake.
Detailed rules: Use a dictionary or word list. The reader secretly copies the real meaning and collects invented definitions on identical slips. Shuffle, number and read all choices. Players secretly vote and cannot choose their own. A correct vote earns two points; each vote for your fake earns one. The reader scores zero that round. After everyone has read once, highest total wins.
Recommendation reasons: Knowing obscure definitions isn't the main advantage. Sounding just authoritative enough to fool your friends can be the more rewarding skill.

Name: Fishbowl
Conclusion: By round three, one silent gesture can call back an entire joke from round one.
Core rules: Two teams guess the same bowl of prompts in three rounds: open verbal clues, one-word clues, then silent mime. Add correct guesses across all rounds; the higher score wins.
Detailed rules: Each player contributes three familiar names or nouns. Alternate one-minute turns, switching clue givers; each solved slip earns one point and stays out until the round ends. Passed or unfinished slips return after the turn. Empty the bowl before resetting all slips for the next restriction. Do not say the answer or parts of it, and do not mouth words in the mime round.
Recommendation reasons: At a big gathering the same names return as descriptions, then as single-word clues and finally as gestures. A name nobody could explain ten minutes ago can suddenly be guessed from a shrug. Choose names everyone knows so newcomers get to share in the jokes.

Name: Five-Card Draw
Conclusion: Everyone gets one chance to redraw. How many cards an opponent keeps is one of the few clues you have.
Core rules: Build the best five-card poker hand after one draw, or win when everyone else folds. Bets use play chips and no community cards are exposed.
Detailed rules: Everyone antes and receives five private cards. After a betting round, remaining players discard any number and draw replacements. Bet again, then show if more than one player remains. Compare straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three, two pair, pair and high card in that order. Break equal categories by card rank, never by suit; split exact ties.
Recommendation reasons: One draw and two betting rounds make this an approachable introduction to poker. Even a beginner can notice the difference between an opponent taking three new cards and taking none.

Name: Flip 7
Conclusion: Six different numbers in front of you make an ordinary decision feel extraordinary: stop safely, or ask for the seventh?
Core rules: Hit or stay on your turn. A duplicate number normally busts you for the round. Seven different number cards end the round immediately with a 15-point bonus. Finish the round in which someone reaches 200; highest total wins.
Detailed rules: The dealer offers face-up cards around the table. Players who stay keep their score for the round; all staying or busting ends it. A Second Chance cancels one duplicate and is discarded with that card; nobody can carry the protection into the next round. Freeze and Flip Three can affect another player. Action and modifier cards never count toward seven numbers. Apply number multipliers before flat bonuses, then add any Flip 7 bonus. Three or more can play; there is no fixed maximum.
Recommendation reasons: For nine people wanting a relaxed game, the table can cheer for a seven-card run without learning much strategy. It is especially easy to play another round with occasional gamers.

Name: Flip 7: With a Vengeance
Conclusion: Here, even another player’s score can be a target. A good hand is not necessarily safe just because its numbers are different.
Core rules: Hit or stay with a standalone deck of altered number and action cards. Duplicates usually bust, but special numbers have exceptions. Seven different numbers normally earn a bonus of fifteen. Highest total at the end of a round reaching 200 wins.
Detailed rules: Zero normally makes the round worth zero unless you Flip 7, and forces you to keep hitting. An Unlucky 7 clears your other numbers and modifiers. A second 13 is allowed; a third busts you. Follow the action cards when they steal, swap or reduce points. Standard rounds cannot score below zero. If everyone chooses Brutal Mode before starting, negative rounds are possible and a Flip 7 can instead take fifteen points from an opponent. Three or more can play; there is no fixed maximum.
Recommendation reasons: Choose it when nine people want the same quick decisions with more mischief. Being able to interfere with someone else’s score, especially in Brutal Mode, is its appeal.

Name: Forehead Poker
Conclusion: Everyone can see the card on your forehead except you. Their reactions are all you get to go on.
Core rules: Hold one card facing outward, then decide whether to stay in or fold. The highest card among players still in wins the play-token pot.
Detailed rules: Give everyone equal tokens and ante one apiece. Deal one unseen card each and hold it above the forehead. Take one round of decisions; if a bet is made, remaining players must match it or fold. Rank ace high down to two and split ties. Move the dealer after each hand; most tokens after the agreed rounds wins.
Recommendation reasons: The reversed information is funny before anyone says a word. Players who dislike memorizing poker hands can still enjoy working out why a friend is smiling.

Name: Fortunately, Unfortunately
Conclusion: Disaster and rescue keep trading places, and every player inherits whatever twist the previous one invented.
Core rules: Build one shared story a sentence at a time, alternating fortunate and unfortunate developments. New events must fit what has already happened. The group finishes the story together.
Detailed rules: Start with a neutral opening sentence and go clockwise. Alternate sentences beginning Fortunately and Unfortunately; elaborate freely but never erase another player's contribution. Allow a pass when someone is stuck. After everyone contributes three times, the final speaker brings the story to a close. There is no individual score.
Recommendation reasons: A setback hands the next player an opportunity to rescue the story. That reliable rhythm makes improvising easier for people who rarely tell stories aloud.

Name: Freeze Dance
Conclusion: A room full of moving bodies suddenly becomes a collection of improbable statues.
Core rules: Dance while music plays and freeze the instant it stops. A designated DJ controls unpredictable stops. A moving or talking player takes a strike; the last dancer remaining wins.
Detailed rules: Clear a space or play with seated upper-body movement. Choose a DJ and start or stop the music without a countdown. Hold each pose until music restarts; three strikes make a dancer a spectator. If the last dancers reach three strikes together, give them one final freeze. Rotate the DJ next round.
Recommendation reasons: Children can practice listening and controlling motion without a long explanation. Sudden freezes also give a group an easy way to laugh together.

Name: Gaia Project
Conclusion: Building beside a rival might help their power supply, yet the same planet may be the link your federation needs.
Core rules: Develop one faction over six rounds by colonising planets, upgrading structures, advancing research and forming federations. Round bonuses, endgame objectives and remaining resources all contribute to the final score.
Detailed rules: Income and the Gaia phase precede the action phase. Pay for range and terraforming when founding mines; upgrade along your faction’s building track. Nearby opponents may pay victory points to charge power. Power cycles through three bowls and is normally spent from the third. A standard federation requires connected structures worth at least seven power; satellites cost permanent power tokens. Passing selects a booster for the next round. Faction abilities can change these costs and conditions.
Recommendation reasons: Four players learning together can discover different approaches on the same crowded map. It suits a group interested in how each faction develops rather than one looking for big swings of luck.

Name: The Gang
Conclusion: Picking up the strongest chip is a statement your partners can read. Putting it down again can tell them even more.
Core rules: Build the best five-card poker hand from two private cards and the community cards. Without revealing card information, use numbered chips to rank the team from weakest to strongest. Three successful heists before three alarms wins.
Detailed rules: Choose rankings through four stages: before community cards, after the three-card flop, after the fourth card and after the fifth. Each stage uses its own chips. Watch how choices change, but do not hint at ranks, suits or deductions that depend on your hand. Reveal hands in final chip order and compare kickers when needed. Players with truly identical best five-card hands may appear in either relative order; their positions against everyone else must still be correct. For the basic heists, use a standard deck and four sets of numbered markers.
Recommendation reasons: With six players, sorting everyone correctly is a real challenge. Watching a teammate repeatedly take and release a chip becomes almost as informative as seeing a card.

Name: Garbage
Conclusion: An early reveal can set off a whole chain of discoveries in your face-down row.
Core rules: Fill numbered positions in your layout from ace through ten. A card you uncover may fill another position immediately; completing a layout means playing with one fewer position in the next round. Finish a one-position layout to win.
Detailed rules: Start with ten face-down cards per person in two rows. Draw from the stock or take the top discard. Place a usable rank in its slot and continue with the card displaced. A king is wild and can move if its proper number later arrives. A jack, queen, duplicate or unusable rank ends the turn as a discard. Redeal after each completed layout.
Recommendation reasons: The positions make number order visible for younger players, while a lucky chain of reveals gives even experienced players a reason to cheer.

Name: Ghost
Conclusion: You must keep a real word possible while steering the fragment toward a word someone else has to finish.
Core rules: Take turns appending one letter to a word fragment. Completing a valid word of at least four letters loses the round; a challenge settles whether a fragment can still become a word.
Detailed rules: Agree on a vocabulary before starting; exclude names, abbreviations and hyphenated words. Instead of adding a letter, challenge the preceding player to give a valid completion. If they can, the challenger loses; otherwise the challenged player loses. Each loss adds the next letter of GHOST; spelling all five eliminates you. Last survivor wins.
Recommendation reasons: It works on the road without supplies, and the fun comes from anticipating the end of a word that nobody has actually said yet.

Name: Gin Rummy
Conclusion: Knocking now can bank a small lead, but it can also let your opponent turn the whole hand against you.
Core rules: Build concealed melds, drawing and discarding one card each turn. Knock at ten or fewer deadwood points or go gin with none; play to 100 points.
Detailed rules: Deal ten each. Aces count one and are low in runs; face cards count ten. After a knock, reveal melds; the defender may lay off onto them unless the knocker has gin. An ordinary win scores the deadwood difference. A defender with equal or less deadwood undercuts for 25 plus the difference; gin earns 25 plus all opposing deadwood. Redeal without scoring if the stock falls to two before a knock.
Recommendation reasons: For two people it offers a compact duel with a real decision about when to stop. Knock while your unmatched cards are low, or risk one more draw to try for gin; the card you discard could be just what the other player is waiting for.

Name: Gloomhaven: Jaws of the Lion
Conclusion: Two cards express a whole turn: one can move you into place, the other can land the attack, and their initiative numbers decide whether the enemy gets there first.
Core rules: Fight a cooperative campaign of linked scenarios with two to four characters. In a normal round each character selects two ability cards and chooses one for initiative. When acting, use the top of one and the bottom of the other. Meet the scenario objective while at least one character can still fight. A solo player controls two characters.
Detailed rules: Reveal monster abilities and act in initiative order. Attack modifier cards adjust damage; monster movement and targeting follow their rules rather than another player's choices. Used cards normally enter the discard pile, while powerful loss actions go to the lost pile. Rest to recover discarded cards at the cost of losing one. A character exhausts at zero health or when unable to play or rest legally. The first five scenarios introduce rules gradually before full character decks and campaign choices come into play.
Recommendation reasons: The opening scenarios teach the card system in pieces. Once it clicks, the same hand offers both a positioning puzzle and a stamina puzzle: spending your strongest effect now leaves fewer turns to finish the job.

Name: Go Fish
Conclusion: Every request gives away a little of the asker’s hand. Remembering who wanted sevens can be as useful as drawing one.
Core rules: Ask one opponent for a rank you hold and collect sets of four. The player with the most completed sets wins.
Detailed rules: Deal seven cards each for two or three players, five for four to six. A player asked for a rank must hand over every card of that rank; a successful asker goes again. If refused, draw from the pond. Drawing the requested rank also earns another turn. Lay down completed books immediately. An empty hand refills from the pond up to its starting size. Once all thirteen books are down, compare totals.
Recommendation reasons: Children can ask an opponent for a rank that they already hold. Remembering what other players have asked for gives them a clue about whom to ask next.

Name: Going to Boston
Conclusion: The best die from each throw stays on the table, giving the youngest players a score they can follow as it grows.
Core rules: Roll three dice and keep the highest; roll the other two and keep the higher one; roll the last die and add all three saved faces. Highest turn total wins the round.
Detailed rules: Go clockwise, giving everyone one complete three-two-one turn. Saved dice may not move again and a tied highest die can be either one. Award a match point to each round leader. Agree on five or ten rounds; highest match score wins, with an extra round available for a tie.
Recommendation reasons: With no strategy barrier, children can start immediately and practice comparing numbers and adding three small values as part of play.

Name: Hadrian’s Wall
Conclusion: Building a stretch of wall can earn the worker you need to finish a market. The question is when to stop extending the chain and start defending your weakest flank.
Core rules: Spend workers and stone on two personal sheets over six years. Develop the fort and town while keeping three cohorts strong enough to repel raids. Score your four attributes and personal goals, then subtract disdain.
Detailed rules: Each year, choose one of two cards as a scoring objective and use the other for supplies. Everyone marks actions simultaneously; a reward can fund another action immediately. At year’s end, reveal the raid cards and check each flank separately. Temple favours can cancel an attack; diplomats protect only their assigned flank. In solo play, two neutral cards stand in for neighbours when trading or scouting. After six years, break a tied score by least disdain, then by points from objectives.
Recommendation reasons: It offers a dense solo puzzle without waiting for anyone else’s turn. That same concentration can feel more like an exam if you want an easy evening.

Name: Hangman
Conclusion: A frequent letter can uncover half the word, while a risky full-word guess can settle the round at once.
Core rules: A word setter shows blanks for the secret word. Guess letters to reveal all their positions, or guess the word outright. Solve it before six mistakes; otherwise the setter wins.
Detailed rules: Choose a familiar word or phrase and show spaces. Guessers take turns naming unused letters. A hit reveals every copy; a miss adds one of six marks to a drawing or progress bar. A wrong full-word guess costs one mark. Do not count repeated letters as new guesses. Rotate the setter between rounds.
Recommendation reasons: With just paper and a pencil, short waiting periods become a vocabulary puzzle. Watching the pattern emerge makes even an incorrect letter informative.

Name: Heads Up!
Conclusion: The person holding the word can't see it; the rest of the room can hardly wait to explain it.
Core rules: Hold a prompt facing outward. Everyone else gives clues while you guess as many prompts as possible in sixty seconds; each correct answer is one point.
Detailed rules: Write familiar words on slips or display them one at a time on a screen. Clues may include examples, associations and sounds but not the answer, its spelling or an obvious inflection. Say pass to replace a difficult prompt without scoring. Rotate guessers so everyone gets one timed turn; compare totals or add team scores.
Recommendation reasons: It puts most of the room on the clue-giving side. A flurry of hints, noises and near guesses creates the lively part of each turn.

Name: Hearts
Conclusion: Usually the queen of spades is a disaster; occasionally you want her and every heart too.
Core rules: Follow suit when possible; the highest card of the led suit takes the trick. Hearts and the queen of spades are penalties. Lowest score wins.
