Detailed rules: Deal thirteen each. Pass three cards left, right, across and then not at all on successive hands. The two of clubs opens. Do not discard penalties on the opening trick or lead hearts before they are broken unless only hearts remain. Hearts cost one each; the queen of spades costs thirteen. Taking all 26 instead gives each opponent 26. End after someone reaches 100.
Recommendation reasons: It is a strong four-person choice with a standard deck. Normally everyone ducks the queen of spades, but a player who seems to be losing might be collecting every penalty card on purpose. Spotting that in time can change the card you play next.

Name: Heat: Pedal to the Metal
Conclusion: Taking a corner fast is easy once. The real decision is how much strain the engine can still absorb at the next bend.
Core rules: Choose a gear and play that many speed cards. Move along the track, paying Heat when you exceed a corner’s limit; if you cannot pay, spin out. After the required laps, finishing positions decide the race.
Detailed rules: Select gears and cards together, then resolve cars in race order. Eligible trailing cars can use adrenaline; a slipstream can move a car two extra spaces without adding to its speed for the corner check. Every corner line crossed still requires a check. Paid Heat moves from the engine to the discard pile and may later clog your hand; cooling returns it to the engine. Cars finishing in the same round compare how far they travelled beyond the line. Solo racing uses Legends opponents.
Recommendation reasons: Six cars bring gear changes, corner limits and the catch-up rule into the same calculation. Get the catch-up rule right: it makes a real difference to how close the race feels.

Name: Herd Mentality
Conclusion: The cleverest answer may be the one that loses you the round. The fun is predicting which ordinary answer this particular group will write down.
Core rules: Read a question aloud and have everyone secretly write a single answer. Reveal together: players who gave the most common answer earn one cow token each. A lone outlier can end up holding the pink cow. Reach eight tokens without holding the pink cow to win.
Detailed rules: If the largest groups are tied, nobody scores and the cow does not move. Otherwise, exactly one person with an answer that no one else wrote takes the pink cow; if several people wrote unique answers, leave it where it is. The holder may keep scoring but cannot win while holding it. If several eligible players reach eight together, raise the target and play on until one leads.
Recommendation reasons: The reveal is especially useful at a big table: everyone has already made a choice, and an everyday question supplies the conversation. No specialist knowledge is needed to discover where the group's intuition splits.

Name: Heredity: The Book of Swan
Conclusion: An injury covers a space where you used to take an action. The family’s condition changes what you can actually do in the next scene.
Core rules: Control the Swan family together. Assign action tokens to explore, interact and fight while a timeline advances events and enemies. Each chapter gives the group its own objectives and ending.
Detailed rules: Open only the numbered cards requested by the chapter. Players decide which character acts next and place a token in an available slot on a character, item or scene. Tests use karma cards and modifiers. Resolve events as the timeline reaches them. Crossing a red line causes one undefended damage; damage covers action slots. If no eligible slot remains and the character must take more damage, resolve a severe injury. Save the cards and changes specified at the end of the chapter.
Recommendation reasons: A good fit for two people who want the story to keep moving. The chapters feel manageable without leaving a campaign set up on a table for weeks.

Name: Hot Seat
Conclusion: For two minutes the whole group gets to follow its curiosity about just one person.
Core rules: Give each person a timed turn answering questions from the group. Anybody may pass on a question; everyone takes one turn before anyone repeats. There is no winner.
Detailed rules: Sit in a circle and choose comfortable topics such as hobbies or imaginary trips. Set two minutes per guest, ask one short question at a time and let the guest decide how much to say. Do not repeat a declined question. Rotate clockwise when time expires and shorten turns for a large group.
Recommendation reasons: On your turn you can start with an easy question and pass on one you would rather not answer. The time limit makes room for everyone to have a turn.

Name: Human Knot
Conclusion: The puzzle is made out of the players themselves: the move that frees one pair of arms may tighten another.
Core rules: Form a knot of joined hands and try to untangle it into a circle without letting go. Everyone wins together if the starting arrangement can be untangled.
Detailed rules: Stand in a circle. Each person takes a free hand from two different people, avoiding immediate neighbors. Talk through stepping over or beneath arms and rotating bodies; move slowly and stop if anyone is uncomfortable. Give it five to ten minutes. Some arrangements cannot form one circle; release and reset instead of forcing them.
Recommendation reasons: Nobody can solve the physical puzzle alone. Explaining where a teammate should turn or step gives a group a concrete reason to communicate.

Name: I Spy
Conclusion: A familiar room changes when you have to notice which object the clue could mean.
Core rules: One player privately chooses a visible object and clues its first letter. Others take turns guessing. A correct guess becomes the next clue giver.
Detailed rules: Keep the object in shared view. The clue giver answers yes or no without changing targets. No leaving the playing area or using a camera to zoom. If everyone has guessed twice without success, give a color or location hint; reveal after one more unsuccessful circuit. Scoring is unnecessary.
Recommendation reasons: It starts and stops easily, uses no materials and invites children to notice details around them rather than stare at a screen.

Name: Incan Gold (Diamant)
Conclusion: The gems already on the path belong to nobody. Leaving just before everyone else can be worth more than discovering another treasure.
Core rules: Explore five caves. Split each treasure among those still inside, leaving the remainder on the path. Before each new card, secretly decide to stay or leave. A second hazard of the same kind wipes out that expedition’s unbanked loot.
Detailed rules: Everyone still inside reveals their decision together. Departing players bank what they carry and divide the leftover path gems among themselves. Players staying behind get none of that share. A hazard never takes treasure already banked at camp. After a failed expedition remove one copy of the hazard that ended it, then prepare the next cave. Most stored treasure after five expeditions wins. In the optional relic game, only a player leaving alone can claim a relic on the path.
Recommendation reasons: At eight, the rules are easy to explain and every new card gives everyone a decision. Watching the group split between running and staying keeps the table lively.

Name: Just a Minute
Conclusion: Even an innocent pause can put another speaker in charge of your unfinished sentence.
Core rules: Talk on a topic for sixty seconds without long hesitation, significant repetition or deviation. Others may challenge; a successful challenger takes over. Whoever is speaking when time expires scores.
Detailed rules: Use an accessible topic and allow no pause longer than two seconds. Common articles and prepositions may repeat. Pause the timer for a challenge, specify the fault and resolve it by group vote or a referee. Resume on the same topic with the remaining time. Rotate starters so everyone begins at least once; highest points wins.
Recommendation reasons: It gives quick thinkers two ways in: improvise a speech or listen closely enough to catch a slip. A minute stays busy for the entire group.

Name: Just One
Conclusion: The obvious clue is often the least useful one, because someone else probably wrote it too.
Core rules: One player guesses while the others independently write a single-word clue. Cancel duplicate and invalid clues before revealing the rest. The group scores for words guessed from a deck of thirteen cards.
Detailed rules: The guesser selects a word number without seeing the card. Clue writers compare boards while the guesser looks away; identical clues and equivalent forms are all removed. A correct guess scores one card. Passing discards only the current card, while a wrong guess also costs the next card if available. In a three-player game each of the two clue givers uses two boards and writes two different clues. Rotate the guesser each round. Paper, pencils and a list of homemade prompts are enough.
Recommendation reasons: At seven, several perfectly sensible clues can disappear at once. Those accidental matches give a pure cooperative game its jokes without anyone having to perform.

Name: Kemps
Conclusion: You want exactly one person to notice what you're doing, while everyone else is watching for the same gesture.
Core rules: Partners privately agree on a gesture. Exchange cards in real time until one partner holds four of a kind, then signal the other to call Kemps before rivals intercept.
Detailed rules: Deal four cards each and expose four in the middle. Exchange one for one, always keeping four; sweep and refresh an unwanted market. Correctly calling your partner's four earns a point. Name an opponent and call Stop Kemps to intercept theirs for a point instead. A mistaken call costs the caller's team one. Redeal after a call; first team to five wins.
Recommendation reasons: Watching the table matters as much as collecting cards. A tiny glance or an exaggerated fake signal can turn a race for four matching cards into a lively guessing game.

Name: King of Tokyo
Conclusion: Inside Tokyo you can hit every monster outside it. Outside Tokyo every monster can hit you. Deciding when to give up the city is often harder than deciding which dice to reroll.
Core rules: Roll six dice up to three times, keeping any results you like between rolls. Matching numbers score points, claws attack, energy buys powers, and hearts heal only outside Tokyo. Win immediately by reaching twenty victory points or being the last monster alive.
Detailed rules: Three matching number faces score the face value; each extra matching die adds one. A monster inside attacks everyone outside, while outside monsters hit those in Tokyo. An occupant damaged by an attack may yield the space to its attacker. Under the standard multiplayer rules entering Tokyo gives one point and starting your turn there gives two. Spend energy on available keep or discard cards and apply their effects. A monster at zero health is eliminated.
Recommendation reasons: The dice give you a quick choice between healing, scoring and attacking. Tokyo gives that choice a consequence the whole table can see: stay for the points, or get out while you still have enough health to recover.

Name: Kings in the Corner
Conclusion: Everyone builds on one solitaire layout, so a move that opens space for you can open space for somebody else too.
Core rules: Play cards in descending, alternating colours. Kings open the four corners. Be first to play all the cards in your hand.
Detailed rules: Deal seven each and reveal four piles around the stock. Draw once, then make any number of legal placements. A whole descending sequence may be moved onto a compatible pile; fill a vacated side with any card or legal sequence. Only kings can start a diagonal corner. When stock is gone, keep playing without drawing. If everyone is blocked, fewest hand cards wins.
Recommendation reasons: It is a good family choice for people who enjoy solitaire but want company. Everyone can follow the same visible puzzle while working on a different hand.

Name: Knockout Whist
Conclusion: Winning a single trick buys you another hand, even when someone else has won every trick so far.
Core rules: Follow suit when possible; highest trump, or highest card of the led suit if no trump appears, takes the trick. Players who win none leave. Hands grow shorter until one player remains.
Detailed rules: Start with seven cards each, turn up the next stock card for trump and have the dealer's left neighbor lead. Each trick winner leads again. Shuffle and rotate deal among survivors; reduce the hand by one down to a single card. If several survive, repeat single-card hands. There is no bidding or extra life in this version.
Recommendation reasons: The shrinking hands make this a short introduction to trick-taking. A modest hand still has a clear job: find one trick you can win.

Name: Left Center Right
Conclusion: Losing your last chip needn't be the end: the next player might send one straight back to you.
Core rules: Roll up to three dice and move chips left, right or into the center as indicated. Keep playing until only one person holds chips; that player wins.
Detailed rules: Give everyone three chips. Roll one die per chip held, up to three. Each one sends a chip left, two sends it right, three sends it to the center; four, five or six keeps it. Resolve the roll together. Center chips never return. Empty-handed players skip their roll but may receive chips before their next turn.
Recommendation reasons: Nobody has to learn a strategy, and even an empty-handed neighbor has a reason to stay involved. The changing fortunes are easy for a large table to follow.

Name: Legends of the Three Kingdoms: Fight the Landlord
Conclusion: Three players get a lopsided duel: the strongest single seat has to outlast two opponents who can help one another.
Core rules: One landlord faces two peasants. Each plays a general with individual abilities and uses attack, defence and support cards. The peasants win by defeating the landlord; the landlord must defeat both peasants.
Detailed rules: Choose roles and generals, then let the landlord take the first turn. Resolve judgement, drawing, playing and discarding in turn order; Dodge can answer an Attack and Peach can rescue a dying general. In this OL ruleset the landlord gets an extra draw during preparation and one extra Attack allowance. At the start of judgement the landlord may discard two cards to clear the judgement area. Apply the chosen generals’ abilities when they change a normal card effect.
Recommendation reasons: It suits three people waiting for a fourth: a short, decisive fight can lead straight into a rematch. Allow longer for generals with elaborate abilities.

Name: Liar’s Dice
Conclusion: The dice you can see are evidence; the number of dice you claim exist tells everyone how far you're willing to bluff.
Core rules: Roll hidden dice and bid on how many of a given face exist across the table. Raise the last claim or challenge it. A wrong bid or wrong challenge costs a die; last player with dice wins.
Detailed rules: Start with five dice per person. Raise by bidding a greater quantity, or the same quantity with a higher face. Ones are ordinary. On a challenge reveal all dice: if the count meets or exceeds the bid, the challenger loses a die; otherwise the bidder does. Reroll after each challenge. The loser of the challenge opens if still in play; skip anyone out of dice.
Recommendation reasons: Five or six people can get a surprising amount of play out of a handful of hidden dice. As the count rises, the odds matter, but so does the friend who paused before raising. Calling the bluff makes everyone want to see the reveal.

Name: Lifeboat
Conclusion: The passenger who helps you win a fight may secretly need somebody else on the boat to die. Everyone wants rescue, but rescue does not pay everyone equally.
Core rules: Each passenger has a public character and secret love and hate cards. A round distributes provisions along the boat, gives conscious passengers one action each, then resolves navigation. Row, take goods or contest a seat, and recruit allies in fights. Rescue comes when the fourth bird marker is present; the highest score wins.
Detailed rules: The passenger closest to the provisions picks before passing the rest on. Rowers can put navigation cards aside; the conscious passenger nearest the navigation deck chooses among those set aside, or reveals the top card if none were saved. Navigation may send people overboard or make them thirsty; each thirst needs water or causes a wound. Wounds equal to a character's size knock them unconscious; more kill them. At rescue, score your survival, whether your love survived and your enemy died, and any valuables that still qualify. Even a dead passenger may score.
Recommendation reasons: For a group that enjoys bargaining and open conflict, a seat is worth fighting over for two different reasons: one end controls supplies, the other can influence navigation. Secret loyalties keep an apparent favour from being a simple exchange.

Name: The Message
Conclusion: Accepting a message might help your team, help someone else or put you one black card from elimination. Even a refusal tells the table something.
Core rules: Pass a hand card as intelligence. Hidden red and blue teams try to collect their own colour, while a neutral agent follows a personal mission. Three black intelligence cards can eliminate a player.
Detailed rules: Draw and use legal action cards before sending intelligence. A cipher travels face down, a document face up, and a direct message goes to a named player. Action cards can intercept or redirect a message at specified moments. Reveal accepted intelligence in front of the recipient; it is no longer a hand card. When a card is sent as intelligence, its printed action does not also fire. Resolve missions, faction collections and black-card effects after delivery.
Recommendation reasons: A favourite choice for a five-player table that already likes hidden identities.

Name: Midnight
Conclusion: Saving a six is tempting, but without a one and a four it is ultimately worthless.
Core rules: Keep at least one die after every roll of six dice. Finish with a reserved one and four to qualify, then score the other four faces. Highest qualifying sum wins the round.
Detailed rules: Roll all still-unreserved dice, lock any number of them and never reroll a locked die. Continue until all six are fixed. A missing one or four means zero; otherwise exclude one of each and count the other four, to a maximum of 24. Give the round winner a point and compare points after five rounds.
Recommendation reasons: Qualifying and chasing high numbers pull in opposite directions, so two players can look at the same roll and keep completely different dice.

Name: Modern Art
Conclusion: You might talk up an artist, sell a painting for a premium and discover that your own sales pitch made someone else richer.
Core rules: Auction paintings by five artists. Each painting determines the auction format; popularity sets its artist’s sale price at the end of the round. After four rounds, most cash wins.
Detailed rules: The auction may be open, once around, sealed bid, fixed price or a double auction. If someone else buys your painting, they pay you; buying your own painting means paying the bank. The fifth painting played for any one artist ends the round without being auctioned, but counts for popularity. Only the three most popular artists pay out that round. A qualifying artist’s earlier values can add to the current price; paintings by the other two artists are worthless for that sale.
Recommendation reasons: Four people can play the market two ways: persuade the room that a painting is worth more, or quietly work out what you can afford. Both approaches fit naturally at the same table.

Name: Most Likely To
Conclusion: The surprise isn't always who got the most votes, but which friends saw the same person in completely different ways.
Core rules: Read a playful Most Likely To prompt and point simultaneously at a consenting player who fits it. Count votes and discuss if desired. Predicting the majority is an optional way to score.
Detailed rules: Use kind, low-stakes prompts. Count to three before showing votes; self-votes count and ties may stand. Being nominated never earns or loses points. If scoring, predict the group's choice before the reveal and reward correct predictions. Rotate readers for ten prompts or until everyone has read one.
Recommendation reasons: Everyone points at once in response to the same lighthearted prompt. A split vote can lead to a conversation if the group enjoys being named and sharing its reasons.

Name: Never Have I Ever
Conclusion: One raised or lowered finger can reveal a shared experience nobody knew they had.
Core rules: Take turns naming something you have never done. Everyone who has done it lowers a finger. Play for the stories or compare fingers after an agreed number of turns.
Detailed rules: Begin with five fingers raised each. Phrase a prompt as something you've never done; anybody for whom it is true that they have done it lowers one finger, including the speaker if applicable. Sharing details is optional, and players with no fingers left may still take turns posing prompts. Highest remaining count wins if scoring.
Recommendation reasons: It quickly uncovers common ground or starts a story, with no cards or drinks required. Friends decide for themselves how much detail to share.

Name: Night of the Ninja
Conclusion: You might switch allegiance, lose your life and still earn honour from your house, all in the same short night.
Core rules: Each round, receive a secret house and rank, draft ninja cards and resolve them in order. The house with the highest-ranking survivors earns honour. House loyalties reset each round, but personal honour carries over.
Detailed rules: Deal three ninja cards to each player. Keep one and pass the rest, then keep one more and discard the last. Spies, tricksters and killers act at their specified times. Compare surviving ranks from highest down; 1 outranks 2. Members of the winning house earn honour even if killed. With an odd player count the independent Ronin also earns honour for surviving. Once anyone reaches ten, highest total wins; tied leaders share victory.
Recommendation reasons: At seven, the appeal is the sudden reversal rather than deep identity deduction. It works well for a couple of lively rounds before moving on.

Name: Nim
Conclusion: Taking a whole pile can feel powerful, but what matters is the arrangement you leave your opponent.
Core rules: Alternate taking any positive number of tokens from exactly one pile. Under normal play, taking the last token wins.
Detailed rules: Make three piles of three, five and seven counters. Choose any nonempty pile and remove one or more items without touching another pile on that turn. No passing or returning counters. Continue until the last item is taken. For another round, alternate who moves first.
Recommendation reasons: The rules take moments, but successive games reveal patterns behind winning positions. It suits players who like discovering why a move works.

Name: Oh Hell
Conclusion: Your best card can become a liability the moment you have already won the number of tricks you predicted.
Core rules: Predict exactly how many tricks you will take. Follow suit and try to hit that prediction rather than simply winning the most tricks.
Detailed rules: Begin with one card per person, increase hand size up to the largest equal deal, then decrease back to one. Turn up the next card for trump if available. The dealer bids last and may not make all bids sum to the available tricks. Highest trump or highest led suit wins a trick. An exact bid scores ten plus the bid; a miss scores zero. Highest total wins.
Recommendation reasons: The pleasure is in making a forecast and then having to defend it. Sometimes losing the final trick is the best play of the hand.

Name: Old Maid
Conclusion: With one card left, fanning your hand for a neighbour can feel more suspenseful than drawing from theirs.
Core rules: Remove one queen, discard equal-rank pairs and draw unseen cards from neighbours. The last player holding the unmatched queen loses.
Detailed rules: Deal all 51 cards and immediately put down matching pairs, regardless of suit. Offer the remaining cards face down to your left neighbour. That player draws one, discards a new pair if possible and offers their own hand to the next person. Skip anyone whose hand is empty. Continue until only the unmatched card remains.
Recommendation reasons: It works with children because the objective is instantly visible: everyone is trying to pass on the same unwanted card.

Name: One-Word Story
Conclusion: Nobody controls the sentence for more than a word, so even the narrator can be surprised by what happens next.
Core rules: Build a shared story clockwise, with each person adding exactly one word on a turn. Keep the developing sentence grammatical and listen to where others take it.
Detailed rules: Choose a theme before starting. Add only one word, without planning aloud or revising earlier words; grammatical repeats are fine. Continue to a complete beginning, middle and ending, or use a five-minute timer. On a turn a player may use The End as a closing exception. The group shares the outcome without scoring.
Recommendation reasons: You only add one word, so you never have to invent the whole plot. Listen to the last player, then decide whether to follow their idea or take the story somewhere unexpected.

Name: Palace
Conclusion: You can arrange the cards everyone can see, but your last three plays are a mystery even to you.
Core rules: Get rid of your hand, then your face-up table cards, then your face-down cards. Play cards at least as high as the top card or pick up the entire pile.
Detailed rules: Deal three face-down, three face-up and three hand cards to each player; swap hand and face-up cards before starting. Play one or more matching ranks. A two resets the required rank; a ten or four consecutive equal ranks clears the pile and grants another turn. Draw back to three while stock lasts. Play the final face-down cards blind; an illegal flip joins the pile you take. First out wins.
Recommendation reasons: It travels well with an ordinary deck. The exposed cards reward planning, and the blind finish gives the players who are trailing a way back into the race.

Name: Pandemic
Conclusion: Removing three cubes can feel productive, but passing a single city card to a teammate may bring the whole team closer to a cure. You can rarely do both before the next infection.
Core rules: The team wins by discovering all four cures. Each player takes up to four actions with a specialist, then draws two player cards and infects cities. Move, treat disease, build a research station or exchange knowledge so the right person can turn a set of city cards into a cure.
Detailed rules: Normally, sharing knowledge requires two specialists in the city named on the card. Discover a cure at a research station by discarding five city cards of its colour, unless your role changes the requirement. An epidemic infects a new city heavily and puts the shuffled infection discard pile back on top. A fourth cube of one colour would cause an outbreak that spreads to neighbouring cities. Lose at the eighth outbreak, if a required cube is unavailable, or if the player deck cannot supply two cards. Cured diseases need not be eradicated to win.
Recommendation reasons: The roles give a group concrete reasons to coordinate. A medic can contain a dangerous cluster while another player saves the few actions needed to meet a teammate and exchange a card. Both jobs serve the same finish line.

Name: Password
Conclusion: You only get one word, and the next team may understand it even better than your partner does.
Core rules: A neutral host shows two clue givers the same secret word. Teams alternate one-word clues and one guess per clue. First correct team scores; first to seven points wins.
Detailed rules: Use ordinary clue words, not the answer, part of it, related word forms, spelling, direct translations, gestures or extra sounds. Allow at most five clue-and-guess exchanges per team, then reveal without points if unsolved. Alternate the starting team and rotate the clue and guess roles.
Recommendation reasons: The single-word limit makes each association matter. Hearing a partner land on the same idea from so little information is the payoff.

Name: Pictionary
Conclusion: A crooked sketch can become the perfect clue if your teammates recognize the one detail that matters.
Core rules: A teammate draws a secret prompt without letters or numbers while their team guesses against the clock. Alternate teams and score one per solved prompt.
Detailed rules: Prepare familiar prompts, pens, paper and a one-minute timer. The drawer may add to the sketch but cannot speak, gesture, spell or write numbers. Agree beforehand whether synonyms count. Discard each prompt, rotate drawers and allow equal turns; use one extra turn each to break a tie.
Recommendation reasons: Nobody needs to be a good artist. Time pressure turns rough shapes and teammates' odd interpretations into part of the fun.

Name: Pig
Conclusion: One more roll can put you in front, but a single one erases everything you've earned this turn.
Core rules: Roll one die repeatedly. Add each non-one to a temporary total and decide after each roll whether to bank it. A one loses the temporary total. First to bank 100 wins.
Detailed rules: Start everyone at zero and pass the die clockwise. Holding moves the entire turn subtotal to the player's permanent score. A one ends that turn immediately but never touches previously banked points. For a shorter game agree on a 50-point target before starting.
Recommendation reasons: It makes the arithmetic of risk easy to feel: the same next roll looks inviting at three points and alarming at nineteen.

Name: Poker Dice
Conclusion: A pair of sixes is a good start, but you must choose whether to protect it or chase a much rarer hand.
Core rules: Build the strongest poker-style hand from five dice in up to three rolls. Compare the final hands to award the round; most round points wins.
Detailed rules: After the first roll reserve any dice and reroll the rest up to twice. Rank five of a kind, four, full house, straight, three, two pair, pair and high die. Within categories compare grouped faces first, then kickers. A 2–6 straight beats 1–5. Tied leaders each get a point; set the number of rounds before play.
Recommendation reasons: Familiar poker combinations make the scoring easy to recognize. The short turns keep the focus on which dice are worth rolling again.

Name: Power Grid
Conclusion: The most connected network can still lose if it runs out of fuel. That makes even an opponent’s coal purchase worth watching.
Core rules: Auction power plants, buy fuel, connect cities and run plants for income. Once a player builds to the endgame threshold, the winner is whoever can power the most of their connected cities, not whoever built the longest network.
Detailed rules: Turn order normally favours the largest network in auctions, but smaller networks buy fuel and build first. Pay the current market price for fuel; plants usually store at most twice their operating requirement. A new city costs both a connection fee and a city slot. On the standard five-player Recharged map, reaching fifteen cities during building triggers the end. Use the plants and fuel already on hand to determine supply; among equally capable networks, most remaining cash wins.
Recommendation reasons: The sequence of bidding, earning and replacing an old plant is easy to follow even as the prices get competitive. Five can share a substantial strategy game without splitting into smaller tables.

Name: President
Conclusion: Finishing order can change the pecking order of the next deal as well as the current one.
Core rules: Lead a single or a set of equal ranks. Others must pass or beat it with the same number of cards. First out becomes President; continue to rank the remaining players.
Detailed rules: Deal all cards; 3 is low and 2 high. Passing does not bar you from re-entering before the trick ends. After every other active player passes consecutively, the last player to play starts a fresh trick. In later deals you may use a rank exchange: last gives first their two best cards for any two back, with a one-card exchange for the next pair of ranks.
Recommendation reasons: The changing table hierarchy gives consecutive hands a social story: today’s President can become the player everyone is trying to unseat.

Name: The Resistance: Avalon
Conclusion: A mission can succeed even with a traitor on it. The question is whether the next proposed team deserves the same trust.
Core rules: Leaders propose quest teams and everyone votes. Approved team members secretly submit success or failure. Evil wins after three failed quests; after three successes, good still has to keep Merlin hidden from the Assassin.
Detailed rules: A team needs more approvals than rejections; a tie rejects it. Pass leadership after rejection. Five consecutive rejected proposals on one quest give evil an immediate win. Good players must submit success, while evil may choose either card. One failure normally ruins a quest, but quest four needs two failures at seven or more players. If good completes three quests, the Assassin names a player: finding Merlin wins for evil. Handwritten role, vote and mission slips and a simple round tracker are enough to play.
Recommendation reasons: A strong seven-player choice for repeated games: nobody is eliminated, so everyone can argue, vote and stay involved right up to the assassination.

Name: Reverse Charades
Conclusion: A whole team silently trying to become one object often produces a scene no single actor would invent.
Core rules: Several teammates mime the same prompt together for one guesser. Score for a correct answer in time and rotate the guesser when that team acts again.
Detailed rules: Make two teams and prepare folded prompts. Set one minute per turn. Everyone except the guesser reads the slip; performers may coordinate by gesture but cannot speak, mouth words or spell. Use one prompt per turn and discard it afterward. Compare points after equal turns, with one extra turn per team for a tie.
Recommendation reasons: On your team’s turn, several people can act out a clue for one teammate. A single gesture can help without anyone having to carry the whole performance alone.

Name: Rock Paper Scissors Tournament
Conclusion: A match that takes seconds can decide who advances, and everyone already knows the three possible moves.
Core rules: Pair players in an elimination bracket. Reveal rock, paper or scissors simultaneously; first to two decisive wins advances. Keep pairing winners until one champion remains.
Detailed rules: Randomize opening pairs and give one random bye if the player count is odd. Rock beats scissors, scissors beat paper and paper beats rock. Replay identical or mistimed reveals without scoring. Run each match to two wins and repeat byes if needed in later rounds. No equipment is needed.
Recommendation reasons: It is an energetic group icebreaker with virtually no teaching. Even a large group can start several quick matches at once.

Name: Root
Conclusion: One faction expands a supply line while another tries to obey an increasingly rigid decree. They share a map without playing the same game.
Core rules: Each faction acts through its own Birdsong, Daylight and Evening phases and scores in its own way. Reach 30 points, or activate a dominance card and meet its control objective instead.
Detailed rules: Rule usually goes to the player with the most warriors and buildings in a clearing. Normal movement requires ruling the origin or destination. In battle the attacker normally takes the higher die and the defender the lower; rolled hits are limited by warriors, and an undefended enemy clearing grants an extra hit. At ten or more points an eligible player may activate a dominance card, permanently abandoning the usual scoring victory. Faction rules can override the common rules, including who wins a tie for control.
Recommendation reasons: Four players get four distinctly different jobs. That variety is the attraction and also the reason to leave time for a longer first teach.

Name: Rummy
Conclusion: A single discard may finish your run or give your neighbour the card they have been waiting for.
Core rules: Draw, lay down or extend sets and runs, then discard. Empty your hand to end the deal; the lowest accumulated penalty wins the match.
Detailed rules: Use one deck for up to four players and two for five or six. Deal ten each to two, seven each to three or four, and six each to five or six. A set has three or four equal ranks; a run has at least three consecutive cards in one suit, ace low. Draw from stock or discard. At the end, opponents count unplayed cards: aces one, faces ten, others face value.
Recommendation reasons: A welcoming first meld game: the same draw-and-discard rhythm gives beginners room to start noticing which cards are useful to opponents.

Name: The Search for Lost Species
Conclusion: A habitat clue that tells you little on its own can settle an entire corner of the island once you combine it with a second animal’s habits.
Core rules: Investigate the island through an app and record which animals can occupy each area. Score for accurate sightings and for locating the lost species together with its habitat. Highest score wins.
Detailed rules: The scientist furthest back on the time track normally acts next, so the length of an action affects who moves again. Survey, use cameras or visit a town to narrow down possibilities on your private sheet. A location attempt must name the target area and correctly identify the contents of two areas adjacent to it; mountains block adjacency. A correct attempt triggers final opportunities according to the time track. In solo play the app also handles a rival scientist, Tini.
Recommendation reasons: It feels like a tougher Sudoku built from animal habits. Playing solo leaves time to reason without racing a human opponent to the answer.

Name: SETI: Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence
Conclusion: A probe flight, an observation and a computer full of data can all point to the same species. Discovering it changes what the rest of the table can do.
Core rules: Run a space agency across five rounds. Launch probes, scan stars and analyse data to find traces of alien life. Discoveries open new ways to score; most points at the end wins.
Detailed rules: Take one main action per turn, with free actions as allowed. Move data from your pool into your computer; when the top row is full, pay one energy to analyse it, clear the computer and mark a trace. The first player to pass in a round rotates the solar system, as does researching technology, so routes may change before a probe moves again. Once you pass, you take no more main actions that round. Score endgame cards and objectives after the fifth round.
Recommendation reasons: Card effects can lead naturally into the next action without a long chain of prerequisites. A few plays still leave room to discover new combinations.

Name: Sevens (Dice)
Conclusion: Six scattered numbers can hide several sevens. Spotting the right grouping is more satisfying than the roll itself.
Core rules: Roll six dice once, remove disjoint groups summing to seven and record the remaining pips as penalties. Lowest total across five rounds wins.
Detailed rules: A group can contain two or more dice: a six and one, or four, two and one, for example. No die can count twice. Choose the combination that leaves the smallest sum, then score the remaining dice with no reroll. Removing all dice scores zero; pass the dice and repeat for five rounds.
Recommendation reasons: Trying different ways to make seven turns mental addition into a small puzzle the whole table can follow.

Name: Sevens (Fan Tan)
Conclusion: The six in your hand may be the gate that somebody else’s entire suit is waiting behind.
Core rules: Start suit rows at seven, then extend them one rank at a time up or down. You must play if able; the first empty hand wins.
Detailed rules: Deal the whole deck as evenly as possible. A seven opens its suit; otherwise add only the next rank at either end of that suit. Aces are low and kings high, with no wraparound. If several plays are legal, choose one; you may pass only if none is legal. Over multiple hands, count a penalty for every card still held when someone goes out.
Recommendation reasons: The layout makes it easy for children to learn, but choosing which legal card to release first gives experienced players a way to hold others up.

Name: Ship, Captain and Crew
Conclusion: A fine cargo is worthless until you have a ship, a captain and a crew to carry it.
Core rules: Within three rolls of five dice, secure a six, five and four in that order. If you qualify, the other two dice are cargo and their sum competes for the round.
Detailed rules: Keep a six for the ship, then a five for the captain, then a four for the crew; all three can qualify on one roll if available together. Frozen dice cannot be rerolled. With time left, keep the cargo or reroll both cargo dice. Failure to qualify scores zero. Each round leader earns one point, including ties; play five rounds.
Recommendation reasons: The nautical order makes the rules easy to remember. Everyone can follow a turn and root for the last missing die before the cargo is counted.

Name: Shut the Box
Conclusion: A roll of eight might cross off the eight, the six and two, or the five and three. The choice shapes every roll that follows.
Core rules: Roll dice and cross out any unused numbers from one through nine whose sum equals the roll. When no legal combination remains for a roll, score the numbers still open as penalties. Lowest total wins.
Detailed rules: Draw nine boxes on paper for each run. Use two dice; when the open numbers total six or less, you may roll just one. Closing everything scores zero. Reset for the next player and give everyone three runs. Break a tie by best single run or share the win; when playing alone, try to lower your total.
Recommendation reasons: Trying several sums for the same roll makes mental arithmetic part of a real decision. Paper boxes work just as well as a wooden set.

Name: Six-Card Golf
Conclusion: Replacing a hidden card can rescue a bad column or spoil a pair you did not know you had.
Core rules: Draw and swap cards in a two-by-three grid to minimise its value. Equal ranks in a vertical pair score zero. Lowest total over nine deals wins.
Detailed rules: Deal six cards face down, then reveal any two of your own. Draw from stock or discard to replace a grid card face up. A stock draw may instead be discarded to expose a hidden card. Once one grid is fully exposed, others get one last turn. Aces cost one, twos minus two, kings zero, jacks and queens ten, and other cards face value. Use two decks at five or six.
Recommendation reasons: It is easy to share at a social table: a lower score is always better, but the facedown grid gives every swap a little suspense.

Name: Skull
Conclusion: A flower and a skull look identical from the back. Nothing forces a player who just laid a skull to bid timidly, which is why even one face-down disc can start an argument.
Core rules: Each player secretly stacks flowers or their skull. Instead of adding a disc, a player may name how many discs they can reveal without finding a skull. Others raise or pass. The highest bidder must reveal from their own stack first, then from the tops of other stacks. Complete two bids, or be the last player with discs, to win.
Detailed rules: Start each round by having everyone put down one disc. Bidding ends the laying phase; a player who passes cannot bid again that round. Reveal top discs one by one until the bid is met or a skull appears. On failure, lose one of your remaining discs: choose it yourself if the skull was yours, otherwise the skull's owner picks one of yours at random. Keep the discarded face secret. With no discs left you are out.
Recommendation reasons: Every higher bid makes the bluff more expensive because the bidder must start with their own discs. One risky reveal gives the whole table something to watch, and a few handwritten discs preserve that tension.

Name: Sky Team
Conclusion: The die your copilot puts on the controls can say “I’ll steady the wings” more clearly than words, especially when words are no longer allowed.
Core rules: Two players are the pilot and copilot landing one aircraft. Plan between rounds, then roll in secret and alternate placing dice in the cockpit without discussing them. Meet the landing conditions together to win.
Detailed rules: Each round both players must place a die on their own axis space and another on their engine space. Axis dice control tilt; engine dice control forward movement. Other actions clear traffic, deploy flaps or landing gear, or set the brakes. Flying into traffic causes a collision. On the final approach, reach the airport with no plane blocking it, level the aircraft, deploy all flaps and gear, and keep speed strictly below the brakes.
Recommendation reasons: The pilots can plan before rolling but cannot explain their dice while placing them. A partner’s first placement can give you a reason to abandon your original plan.

Name: Slapjack
Conclusion: A jack changes the rhythm of an ordinary card flip in an instant.
Core rules: Turn cards onto a shared pile. The first player to slap a jack collects the pile; win by collecting all the cards.
Detailed rules: Deal the deck face down and flip away from yourself so nobody sees the card early. The first hand touching a jack takes the pile underneath its stack. Slapping another rank costs one card, given to the player who revealed it. Someone who runs out has one chance to win the next jack before leaving play.
Recommendation reasons: Good for a lively table that wants instant action. Everyone watches every flip, and a mistimed slap is often part of the fun.

Name: Snap
Conclusion: The match may appear on somebody else’s pile, so every player has a reason to watch every card.
Core rules: Reveal onto separate piles. When two exposed ranks match, the first correct call of “Snap!” wins those piles. Collect all the cards to win.
Detailed rules: Deal evenly into unseen stocks. If three top ranks match, the caller takes all matching piles. A wrong call sends the caller’s exposed pile to the centre; the next correct caller also takes it. Turn over an exhausted face-up pile to replenish your stock without rearranging it. A player with neither pile leaves play.
Recommendation reasons: Quick visual matching gives children and adults a shared challenge. Waiting for a turn to flip never means waiting for a turn to play.

Name: SOS
Conclusion: An innocent-looking O can complete several lines at once, including a line the other player thought they were setting up.
Core rules: Write either S or O in an empty grid cell. Score each new straight S-O-S that uses your letter and take another turn if you scored. When the grid fills, highest score wins.
Detailed rules: Use a five-by-five board. Look in horizontal, vertical and both diagonal directions for three adjacent letters. Mark every newly created sequence before the next move; overlapping lines count separately but never score an old sequence twice. Without a new sequence, pass clockwise. Placed letters cannot change.
Recommendation reasons: Only two letters are needed, yet the ability to set a trap or build a chain gives experienced players plenty to see in an almost empty grid.

Name: Spades
Conclusion: A hand is only half a promise: the other half is whether your partner can cover the tricks you bid together.
Core rules: Partners combine their trick bids. Follow the led suit if possible; spades are always trump. Meet the team contract while avoiding costly extra tricks.
Detailed rules: Deal thirteen each. The highest trump wins, otherwise highest of the led suit. Do not lead spades until broken unless holding only spades. A made bid scores ten per contracted trick and one per extra; missing loses ten per contracted trick. Ten extra tricks cost 100. An individual nil bid gains or loses 100. End a hand at 500 or more and compare team scores.
Recommendation reasons: At four, your bid and your partner’s must work as a pair. Deciding which tricks to leave for your partner keeps both players involved even when neither has a strong hand.

Name: Speed
Conclusion: Both players race for the same two piles, so the card you were about to play can become useless in an instant.
Core rules: Play simultaneously from a five-card hand onto either central pile, placing a card exactly one rank higher or lower. Refill from your stock and be first to empty both stock and hand.
Detailed rules: Give each player five hand cards and a fifteen-card stock. Set up two single starting cards and two five-card reserve piles. Suits do not matter and the ace connects king and two. Play one card at a time and refill to five while possible. When both players are stuck, turn one reserve card onto each middle pile; recycle spent middle cards if the reserves run out.
Recommendation reasons: There is no waiting for an opponent to take a turn. A player who spots a short run can unload several cards before the other person reacts.

Name: Spirit Island
Conclusion: You can see which lands are about to be attacked, but your spirit may be better at pushing towns away than destroying them. A neighbour's power can turn that displacement into a defence neither of you could manage alone.
Core rules: Each player controls a different spirit defending the island. Grow, gain energy and play powers, then resolve fast powers, the invaders' actions and slow powers. Generate fear to weaken the invaders' hold and make the current victory condition easier to meet. The spirits win or lose together.
Detailed rules: Presence sets your reach and uncovering it from your spirit board improves your options. Invaders normally ravage, build and explore in the terrain shown by their cards, so an explored land can become next turn's building site. Initially remove all invaders to win; later terror levels require no towns or cities, then no cities, and exhausting the fear deck wins outright. Lose if a spirit loses all presence on the island, the island runs out of blight under its blight rules, or an Invader Card must be drawn from an empty deck.
Recommendation reasons: Different spirits make coordination concrete. One can prevent the next build while another invests in a slow power that pays off later. The visible invader sequence gives the group enough information to plan those moves together.

Name: Spit
Conclusion: Unlike a race from a hand of cards, Spit makes you uncover your next options from five little stacks.
Core rules: Play exposed tableau cards simultaneously onto either middle pile, always one rank higher or lower. Race to clear your tableau, take a middle pile and redeal until someone sheds all their cards.
Detailed rules: Divide the deck in half. Each player builds five piles of one through five cards, tops face up; the rest are a spit stock. Start each center pile with a stock card. An ace touches king and two. Turn up a newly uncovered card and move exposed cards to empty spaces when useful. If both stall, add fresh stocks to the center. On clearing a tableau, claim a middle pile, preferably the smaller one; combine what you took with your remaining cards and redeal.
Recommendation reasons: It works well for two players who enjoy constant action. Clearing an awkward pile can matter as much as spotting the next legal card first.

Name: Splendor
Conclusion: At first you pay for almost everything in gems. Several purchases later a card that once looked unaffordable can cost you nothing at all.
Core rules: On your turn take gem tokens, buy a development, or reserve a card. Each bought card gives a permanent discount in one colour; some also give prestige. When someone reaches 15 prestige, finish the round so everyone has had the same number of turns. Highest prestige wins.
Detailed rules: Take up to three different colours, or two of one colour only if at least four tokens of that colour were available. End your turn with at most ten tokens. Reserving a visible card or the top card of a deck may also earn one gold joker; you can reserve at most three cards. Buy from the display or your reserve. At turn end a visiting noble gives prestige if you have the required permanent bonuses; choose one if several qualify. Break a prestige tie in favour of fewer bought developments.
Recommendation reasons: The choice between buying a modest discount now and reserving an expensive card before an opponent does is easy to grasp. Because the discount lasts, you can see precisely how an early purchase opened up a later one.

Name: Spoons
Conclusion: A player taking a spoon as quietly as possible can start a scramble before anyone notices their cards.
Core rules: Pass cards to collect four of a kind. Once someone takes a spoon, everyone may take one. The player left empty-handed loses the round.
Detailed rules: Use one fewer spoon than players and deal four cards each. The dealer draws one and passes an unwanted card left; each player similarly keeps four and passes one. The last player discards. Only someone holding four of a kind may initiate a grab. For a knockout match, remove the loser and one spoon, then redeal; for a casual round simply restart together.
Recommendation reasons: The first player can take a spoon quietly, then everyone reaches as soon as they notice. A deck of ordinary cards and a few spoons are enough for that sudden change of pace.

Name: Sprouts
Conclusion: A single curve both spends room and creates a fresh dot. A harmless-looking line can divide the board into separate problems.
Core rules: Connect dots without crossing existing lines, then add a new dot on the curve. No dot can have more than three incident line ends. In a duel, whoever draws the last legal line wins.
Detailed rules: Start with five dots. A move may join two dots or loop back to one; a loop uses two ends at its starting dot. Do not pass through a third dot or cross your own line. The new dot already has two ends. When no legal move remains, the next player loses; the two-player game gives the clearest contest. For three or four, the player unable to move is eliminated and the survivors restart.
Recommendation reasons: Very few rules generate surprisingly intricate shapes. Children can draw freely while experienced players work out which regions will run out of moves first.

Name: Spyfall
Conclusion: An answer must reassure the people who know the location without teaching the one person who doesn't.
Core rules: Everyone except the spy learns the same location. Players question one another to expose the spy while the spy listens for the location. Find the spy or name the location to win for your side.
Detailed rules: In this paper version, one neutral host prepares matching location slips and one spy slip for the active players. Set six minutes. Ask another player; that person answers and questions someone other than the previous asker. Never name the location in an answer. A majority accusation exposes the target and ends the game; a wrong target wins for the spy. The spy has one location guess, losing if wrong, and wins if time runs out.
Recommendation reasons: It gives a talkative group a deduction game without long speeches. A good question tests whether someone knows the place; ask too specifically and you might give the spy enough to name it. Both sides have a reason to listen to every answer.

Name: Sushi Go Party!
Conclusion: The dumpling that looks unremarkable now may make a whole set pay off. But the hand travels around the table, and someone can take the next dumpling before it returns.
Core rules: Choose a menu for the game. Over three rounds, everyone secretly picks one card from their hand, reveals together and passes the rest on. Score the dishes you collected by their own rules; save dessert for the end. Highest total wins.
Detailed rules: Nigiri is always on the menu; add one roll, three appetizers, two specials and one dessert, observing the player limits printed for particular dishes. Deal the hand size for the player count and pass to the left. Some dishes score immediately at round end, some need pairs or sets, and others depend on what the table collected. Keep desserts across rounds, shuffle the non-dessert cards back in, and add the next round's desserts. If final scores tie, more dessert cards breaks the tie.
Recommendation reasons: The turn itself stays short even around a large table: everyone makes one choice at the same time. Changing a dish on the menu changes what is worth keeping, so a second game asks different questions without reteaching the draft.

Name: Taboo
Conclusion: When all the obvious words are forbidden, an everyday object suddenly needs an inventive description.
Core rules: Give spoken clues for a target without using it or its forbidden words. Teammates guess as many targets as possible within a minute; the higher team score wins.
Detailed rules: Make cards with one target and five related forbidden words. An opponent monitors each card. No spelling, gestures, rhymes or close word forms. Correct answers earn one point and reveal a fresh card; a forbidden word, pass or timeout discards the card without a point. Rotate clue givers and give teams equal turns.
Recommendation reasons: Working around banned words produces unexpected descriptions, and everyone can tell exactly why an apparently easy clue became difficult.

Name: Tag Team
Conclusion: Once an attack goes into your deck, you know when it will return. The problem is whether it will meet a block this time.
Core rules: Each player pairs two fighters and reveals fight cards simultaneously. Between rounds, insert one new card without changing the old order. Normally, knocking out either opposing fighter wins.
Detailed rules: Start with one fight card from each fighter. Resolve both revealed cards together, applying damage, blocks and fighter-specific effects. When the fight deck is spent, draw three build cards and insert one into the deck without shuffling it. Resolve a double knockout on opposing teams as a draw. If a build deck can no longer supply three cards, the fight is also a draw. Individual fighter abilities may explicitly alter a knockout result.
Recommendation reasons: Pairing fighters is only half the duel. Fixed card order makes timing an attack or a block feel like calling a move in a fighting game.

Name: Telephone
Conclusion: The last sentence is funny because everyone was trying to pass on exactly the same thing.
Core rules: Whisper a sentence through a chain of listeners, once per person. Compare the final public version with the original; the basic game has no individual winner.
Detailed rules: Sit in a line or circle. Start with a sentence of roughly eight to twelve words and whisper only to the next person. Do not repeat, correct, take notes or consult earlier speakers. The last listener speaks aloud, then the starter reveals the original. Change who starts for the next round.
Recommendation reasons: Even small mishearings compound along the line. Comparing the two endpoints gives a whole group a shared joke with no preparation.

Name: Telephone Pictionary
Conclusion: The phrase becomes a picture, the picture becomes a new phrase, and neither has to resemble the original for long.
Core rules: Pass paper packets around the table, alternating between drawing the last phrase and writing what the last drawing depicts. Reveal each full chain at the end.
Detailed rules: Each person starts a packet with a phrase and passes left. Look only at the newest entry, make the opposite kind of entry on a fresh page, hide the preceding page and pass again. Continue until packets have gone around. Read every packet in order; no scoring is needed.
Recommendation reasons: It is an especially good choice for a big table: everyone draws or writes at once, nobody drops out, and an unrecognisable sketch can improve the round. The payoff is opening the chain and finding the exact picture that turned an ordinary sentence into something else.

Name: Terraforming Mars
Conclusion: A project can raise an entire planet's temperature or feed a small production chain that pays off generations later. Both ambitions compete for the same company's money.
Core rules: Run a corporation, play projects and place tiles as the table raises oxygen to 14%, temperature to +8°C and places nine oceans. Generations end with production. In multiplayer, once all three targets are met, finish that generation; terraforming rating plus points from cards, the map, milestones and awards determines the winner.
Detailed rules: On each turn take one or two actions, or pass for the rest of the generation. New projects cost money to keep and more to play; symbols and global conditions can affect when a project is legal or what later cards are worth. Standard projects offer an alternative to cards. Greenery can raise oxygen, and each city scores for adjacent greenery regardless of who owns it. In the original solo challenge, complete all three global targets by the end of generation fourteen.
Recommendation reasons: The project cards let you build an economy with its own character, while the shared planet sets a deadline no company controls alone. A production upgrade that looks excellent in a long game may arrive one generation too late.

Name: Terrorscape
Conclusion: The killer can hear the survivors planning on the other side of the screen. A perfectly sensible conversation can give away more than a noise token does.
Core rules: One killer hunts three survivor characters on separate maps. The survivors must escape together or hold out for rescue; eliminating any one survivor gives the killer victory.
Detailed rules: With fewer than four people, the survivor side shares control of all three characters. Move, search, clear obstacles or repair the radio, reporting noise when an action requires it. A search can reveal an encounter; resolve its attacks and defences with the relevant cards. To escape at the main exit, all three survivors must gather there with five keys. The hidden exit also needs the secret map. Repairing the radio starts a rescue countdown instead, with no need to gather at a door.
Recommendation reasons: It is particularly lively with one player at each survivor seat. Once the group knows the game, something said within the killer’s hearing can be either a mistake or a deliberate decoy.

Name: Texas Hold’em
Conclusion: Five cards belong to everybody. The question is what the two cards nobody else sees can add to them.
Core rules: Use any five of your two private cards and five community cards to make the best poker hand, or win the pot when everyone else folds. Play with equal stacks of play chips.
Detailed rules: Post the two blinds and deal two hole cards each. Bet before the flop, after three community cards, after the fourth card and after the fifth, burning one card before each reveal. Call, fold, check when nothing is owed or raise within your stack. At showdown compare standard poker hands; identical hands split. An all-in player can win only pots they contributed to.
Recommendation reasons: Using play chips, a table can enjoy the same central puzzle: everyone sees the same community cards, but a check or raise tells a different story depending on who makes it. A new card can strengthen your hand and make an opponent’s earlier bet look quite different.

Name: Thirty-One
Conclusion: Knocking does not claim you have the best hand. It only says you think somebody else is worse.
Core rules: Improve a three-card hand by drawing and discarding. Count only one suit toward 31. Knock to give everyone else a final turn; the lowest hand loses a life.
Detailed rules: Start with three lives each. Aces are eleven, faces ten. Draw the top stock or discard and keep three cards; instead of drawing you may knock. Show 31 immediately to make every other player lose a life. Otherwise compare each player’s best single suit after the final turns; all tied for lowest lose a life. Eliminate players at zero lives and play to one survivor.
Recommendation reasons: Three cards and one scoring suit keep it accessible across ages. The decision to knock gives a short draw-and-discard game a little tension.

Name: Three or More
Conclusion: A pair isn't a score yet. It buys you one last chance to turn the roll into something better.
Core rules: Roll five dice and score matching groups: three equal faces earn three points, four earn six, five earn twelve. A pair alone can earn one reroll. First to twenty wins.
Detailed rules: If the first roll already has three or more alike, score its largest group immediately. If it has a pair but no triple, save one pair and reroll the other three exactly once. Score the largest resulting group, or zero if it still falls short. Five distinct faces end the turn at zero.
Recommendation reasons: In this version, a lone pair gives you one chance to chase a triple. An opening three of a kind or better scores immediately, so it is easy to see what each roll is trying to achieve.

Name: Ticket to Ride
Conclusion: You need one more red card for the long route. The player before you has just started building toward the same junction.
Core rules: Collect coloured train cards and spend matching sets to claim routes on a shared map of North America. Score the routes you build and connect cities on secret tickets. Highest final score wins.
Detailed rules: On a turn draw train cards, claim one route, or draw three destination tickets and keep at least one. Normally take two train cards; a face-up locomotive taken as the first card ends the draw. Match the route’s length and colour, using locomotives as wilds; grey routes accept any one colour. With two or three, only one line of a double route may be claimed. When someone ends a turn with two trains or fewer, everyone gets one final turn. Add completed tickets, subtract failed ones and award the longest-path bonus.
Recommendation reasons: A ticket gives newcomers a concrete destination. Experienced players still have to judge whether to collect more cards or claim a route before someone blocks it.

Name: Tic-Tac-Toe
Conclusion: Every mark has two jobs: build your own three and keep the other player from finishing theirs.
Core rules: Alternate placing X and O on a three-by-three grid. First to make a row, column or diagonal of three wins; a full board without one is a draw.
Detailed rules: X goes first. Place one mark only in an empty square, then immediately check the three rows, three columns and two main diagonals. Stop on a win; symbols cannot be overwritten or moved. Alternate the first player over repeated rounds.
Recommendation reasons: It fills short waits and gives children a clear first lesson in blocking threats. A finished round is brief enough to try a different opening immediately.

Name: Time Bomb
Conclusion: You know what wires you hold, but not where they lie. The person you trust with a cut may also get the next choice.
Core rules: Sherlock’s team must find all the defusing wires within four rounds. Moriarty’s team wins if the bomb is cut or time expires. The cutter always selects another player’s hidden wire; that player takes the cutter next.
Detailed rules: Deal five wires each. Look at their composition, then shuffle your own wires before laying them face down. Players may claim or misrepresent what they have. A harmless wire has no effect; a defusing wire counts toward the team total. End each round after as many cuts as there are players, regardless of who held the cutter. Shuffle and redistribute the remaining wires. With four or seven players, one role is undealt, so the exact team split is uncertain. Homemade role slips, three types of wire cards and a token for the cutters are sufficient.
Recommendation reasons: Easy rules leave room for the table’s jokes, but neither the wire choice nor the handoff is automatic. At six, both decisions make you read what the others are telling you.

Name: Top Ten
Conclusion: Two people can give wildly different answers to the same question and both be right. The puzzle is how intense each meant their answer to be.
Core rules: Give an answer to a prompt that matches your secret number from one to ten. A captain orders the answers from low to high. Keep at least one team token through five rounds to win together.
Detailed rules: The captain chooses a prompt. Nobody may give away a number directly or indirectly. Reveal numbers one at a time in the captain’s chosen order; lose a token whenever a number is lower than the immediately preceding one. Thus 4, 2, 3 costs one token, not two. At four to eight the captain also answers. At nine, only the other eight answer and the team starts with eight tokens. The captain changes each round. Make your own situation prompts and number slips to play without the box.
Recommendation reasons: Good at eight when the point of game night is getting everyone talking. A prompt often starts a conversation that lasts beyond the round.

Name: Toy Battle
Conclusion: The route to an enemy base can also be the last side of a region you need for a medal. Your opponent cannot always defend both.
Core rules: Draw troops or deploy one along a route connected to your headquarters. Capture the enemy headquarters or claim the terrain’s required number of medals to win immediately.
Detailed rules: Choose a terrain and give each side its starting troops. Draw up to two troops into a rack that holds at most eight, or place a troop from the rack. A placement normally needs a continuous line of friendly bases to headquarters; taking an occupied enemy base usually needs a stronger troop. Resolve the troop’s ability and collect medals from regions you surround. If you cannot act, compare medals; a tie goes to the opponent of the player who ended the game.
Recommendation reasons: The draw can feel swingy at first. Different maps make it clearer how much a well-chosen deployment can change the result.

Name: Truth or Dare
Conclusion: The group supplies the surprises, and every player gets to choose what kind of surprise they want.
Core rules: Choose truth or dare and receive a question or a short challenge. Answer, perform, request an alternative or pass. The usual aim is sharing surprises, without a score.
Detailed rules: Agree on the tone of prompts before beginning. An active player can switch category once or pass with no penalty. After a completed prompt, choose the next player while giving everyone turns. Keep challenges brief and easy to decline; there is no need to rank personal answers.
Recommendation reasons: Friends can choose the tone of their questions and challenges. In this version a player can pass without a penalty and let the next person take a turn.

Name: Twenty Questions
Conclusion: One well-chosen question can rule out half the possibilities; one lucky guess can throw away a turn.
Core rules: One thinker chooses a familiar subject. The group has at most twenty yes-or-no questions to identify it, with direct guesses counting toward the limit.
Detailed rules: Announce a category such as people, places or objects. The thinker answers truthfully and may say sometimes or unknown when necessary. Let questioners confer, but count one spoken question at a time and avoid outside searches. Guess correctly within twenty and the group wins; otherwise reveal the answer and rotate the thinker.
Recommendation reasons: It needs no supplies and suits travel or waiting time. Narrowing a category together rewards curiosity more than recalling a single obscure fact.

Name: Two Truths and a Lie
Conclusion: The least believable statement sometimes turns out to be the only one everyone wants to hear more about.
Core rules: Each speaker tells three short things about themselves, exactly two true and one false. Listeners vote for the lie before the speaker reveals it.
Detailed rules: Prepare statements on any topics you are comfortable sharing and deliver them in any order. Allow a short round of questions, then vote simultaneously by showing one, two or three fingers. Rotate speakers. For a score, give correct listeners one point and give the speaker one if nobody spots the lie.
Recommendation reasons: It gives strangers a ready-made conversation starter, and old friends often discover that what they thought they knew about each other was wrong.

Name: Two-Dice Pig
Conclusion: Two dice create two different hazards: a single one spoils the turn, but double ones threaten your whole score.
Core rules: Roll two dice and bank accumulated sums whenever you choose. A single one loses the unbanked turn score; double ones also reset your permanent score. First to bank 100 wins.
Detailed rules: Start at zero and take turns clockwise. If neither die shows one, add their sum and hold or roll again. Non-one doubles have no special effect. After either kind of bust, pass immediately. Scores already banked stay safe on a single one but not on double ones.
Recommendation reasons: In this variant, one 1 costs your turn total and double 1 costs your banked score as well. That gives a player in the lead a different reason to stop rolling.

Name: Ultimate Tic-Tac-Toe
Conclusion: The little square you choose also chooses the next board for your opponent. A local win can send them exactly where they wanted to go.
Core rules: Play tic-tac-toe across nine small boards. Your cell's position directs the opponent to the corresponding board. Win three small boards in a straight line to win the match.
Detailed rules: Start anywhere on the first move. The top-right cell, for example, sends the next move to the top-right small board. Close a local board once won or drawn; if sent to a closed board, choose any open one. Never overwrite a mark or play in a closed board. If all boards close without a global line, draw.
Recommendation reasons: Planning has two levels: what you can accomplish now and what you force your opponent to play next. That gives familiar tic-tac-toe room for real tactics.

Name: Unlock!
Conclusion: Two pictures with nothing obvious in common can unlock an entirely new room. The best discoveries often start with an overlooked detail.
Core rules: Explore an adventure using its numbered cards and companion app. Reveal only the cards you discover, combine objects, operate machines and solve the scenario’s final puzzle.
Detailed rules: Leave the deck in order and start the selected adventure in the app. Read the starting card and reveal only the numbers it directs you to. Certain red and blue objects combine by adding their numbers; other puzzles use hidden numbers, codes or an on-screen machine. Discard cards when instructed. Hints can unstick the group, while wrong codes or penalties may cost time. Finish when the scenario confirms its objective; a replay reveals solutions you already know.
Recommendation reasons: Solo play lets you linger over an unexpected interaction without anyone reading the next card ahead of you. It is an escape room you can unravel at your own pace.

Name: UNO
Conclusion: A single action card can reverse the order or make a neighbor draw just when they thought they were about to finish.
Core rules: Match the discard by color, number or symbol, or play a wild. Draw when you cannot or choose not to play. Empty your hand to win the round and announce UNO when one card remains.
Detailed rules: Deal seven each. A drawn card can be played immediately if legal. Skip costs the next player a turn; Reverse changes direction; Draw Two makes the next player draw two and skip. Wild selects the color. Wild Draw Four is legal only without a card matching the current color: a successful challenge makes its user draw four, a failed challenge costs six. No stacking. Missing UNO and getting caught before the next turn starts costs two cards.
Recommendation reasons: Matching a colour or number is enough to get children and adults playing together. Once somebody is down to one card, everyone watches the turn order: a skip or reverse can stop that player from finishing just when they expect to go out.

Name: War
Conclusion: One tied pair can turn a routine comparison into a contest for a much bigger pile.
Core rules: Both players reveal one card at a time; higher rank takes the pair. Ties start a war for the whole pile. Collect every card to win.
Detailed rules: Deal 26 face-down cards each; aces are high. Put won cards underneath your stack without sorting. On a tie each player adds three face down and one face up, repeating if necessary. If short of cards, use what remains with the last one face up. A shorter game can end at a set time, with the larger stack winning.
Recommendation reasons: It makes comparing numbers tangible for beginners, with the drama of a tie and no strategy for a child to remember.

Name: Wavelength
Conclusion: “Coffee” sounds like an obvious clue for something hot, right up until half the team pictures an iced latte.
Core rules: A clue giver sees a hidden target between two extremes and gives an example that belongs at that point. Teammates decide where to set the pointer. Reveal the target and score for accuracy. In team play the first score of ten triggers the end.
Detailed rules: Choose a spectrum such as easy to hard. Only the clue giver sees the target and may not reveal its position with a number. After the active team settles on a position, the other team predicts which side of the pointer contains the bullseye for a possible bonus. A bullseye scores four; if the active team still trails after hitting it, it gets a catch-up turn. Small groups can play cooperatively. A paper dial with a movable pointer, a hidden target and the same scoring bands can replace the physical dial.
Recommendation reasons: The same example can land at very different points on different people’s scales. Discussing why it belongs there matters more than knowing a piece of trivia.

Name: Welcome to the Moon
Conclusion: Everyone sees the same three options, yet the colonies on two neighbouring sheets can develop in completely different directions.
Core rules: Choose one public number-and-action pair each round, write the number legally on your adventure board and use the paired effect if possible. Missions, the end condition and scoring depend on the adventure.
Detailed rules: Several players may choose the same pair, but nobody may take a number from one pair and an action from another. If any number can be written legally, choose a legal one; otherwise mark a system error. Completing a mission early can affect its reward. Check the current board for its finish triggers and error penalties. Adventures can be played individually or as a linked campaign, and solo play uses an opponent rather than another player’s sheet.
Recommendation reasons: Six people can work at once. The linked adventures add a storyline, while a well-timed chain of effects makes the number puzzle feel rewarding.

Name: Werewolf
Conclusion: By day, the village hears everyone’s account of a night only a few people witnessed. Spotting a lie and persuading the others to vote on it are two different skills.
Core rules: A non-playing moderator alternates secret night actions with daytime discussions and elimination votes.
