Villagers win by eliminating all wolves; wolves win as soon as they equal or outnumber the surviving villagers. Mafia uses this same structure with different roles. The listed headcounts include the moderator.
Detailed rules: Choose one role set before dealing. With eight active players, the werewolf version can use two wolves, a seer, a hunter and four villagers. Wolves pick a victim together; the seer privately checks a player. An eliminated hunter may take one living player with them before victory is checked. For the Mafia variant, use killers, a detective who checks identities and a doctor who can protect the night’s target instead. At dawn announce any victim, then discuss and vote. In this version, revote a tie once; a second tie means no elimination. Eliminated players no longer speak or vote.
Recommendation reasons: Handwritten roles are enough for a table that enjoys listening and persuasion. In either role set, a player with a real clue still has to make others believe it. Choose it when someone wants to moderate and the group is comfortable with player elimination.

Name: Werewords
Conclusion: Finding the secret word is not the end of the mystery. The person who guided everyone there may just have revealed the Seer.
Core rules: Ask the Mayor yes-or-no questions to find a secret word before time runs out. If it is found, the werewolves still win by identifying the Seer; if it is not, the village can still win by finding a werewolf.
Detailed rules: Use the app for nighttime information and the timer. The Mayor also holds a hidden role and answers with tokens rather than explanations. The Seer and werewolves know the word but have different aims. If time expires, discuss and vote; a tied top vote can reveal several suspects. At seven or more, a second werewolf is optional. In that setup, when the word is found each wolf can name a Seer suspect; finding either wolf can save the village when the word was missed. Handwritten roles and simple answer tokens can replace the boxed pieces.
Recommendation reasons: Seven is a good fit for people who enjoy both wordplay and hidden roles. Either side can recover from what looked like a loss, so the last guess still matters.

Name: Who Am I?
Conclusion: Everybody knows who you are except you; a single yes can buy just the follow-up question you need.
Core rules: Wear a hidden identity that everyone else can see. Ask yes-or-no questions about yourself; a yes lets you ask again, while a no passes the turn. Identify your note to finish.
Detailed rules: Write recognizable names or roles for other players without showing recipients their own notes. Give truthful answers and do not volunteer hints. A guess can replace a question; an incorrect guess passes play. Continue until everyone solves their note, or set a time limit and rotate identities.
Recommendation reasons: It gives the table a shared joke without leaving the guesser passive: well-chosen questions can turn a completely blank start into a confident guess.

Name: Wingspan
Conclusion: The first bird in a habitat does a little work. Several birds later the same action might lay eggs, tuck a card and feed a future turn, all in one pass along the row.
Core rules: Across four rounds, take one action per turn: play a bird in a permitted habitat, gain food in the forest, lay eggs in the grassland, or draw bird cards in the wetland. Birds improve the action rows and may activate powers. Score birds, eggs, cached food, tucked cards, round goals and bonus cards; highest total wins.
Detailed rules: Pay a bird's food cost and any egg cost shown for its column. When using a habitat action, take the benefit visible in its first empty space, then work right to left through the birds in that row, optionally using brown powers. Other powers trigger on placement or between turns as printed. At each round end, commit an action cube to the goal board, leaving one fewer action for the next round. Solo uses the Automa deck to provide an opponent and competing scores.
Recommendation reasons: Your early bird choices keep doing work on later turns. That makes the growing chain easy to see, and the different powers give you a reason to build a different habitat the next time you play.

Name: Wink Murder
Conclusion: A wink is enough to remove a player, provided the detective was looking somewhere else.
Core rules: A hidden murderer winks at citizens while a detective tries to identify them. The detective and citizens win on a correct accusation; the murderer wins by exhausting the detective's chances or eliminating all citizens.
Detailed rules: Deal one murderer, one detective and the remaining citizens as secret slips. Sit where faces are visible. A winked citizen silently counts to five before announcing they are out, without pointing at the culprit. The detective may make three accusations. A wrong suspect stays active and keeps their identity hidden. Reveal and redeal afterward.
Recommendation reasons: The delayed collapse and furtive eye contact can be as entertaining as the deduction itself. Everybody has a reason to watch the whole circle.

Name: Word Association Chain
Conclusion: A chain can go from beach to desert in two words, revealing a connection that made sense to only one person at first.
Core rules: In turn, say a new word associated with the immediately preceding one. Repetition, excessive hesitation or an association the group rejects earns a penalty. Fewest penalties wins.
Detailed rules: Start with a familiar seed word and count three seconds per answer. A challenged link may be explained briefly and accepted by majority vote. A failed turn restarts the chain with a fresh seed. Finish after everyone has taken at least five turns or ten minutes have passed; a five-second limit is a gentler option.
Recommendation reasons: It combines quick listening with imagination: somebody else's apparently strange answer can make perfect sense once they explain it.

Name: Would You Rather?
Conclusion: A split vote can be more interesting than a unanimous one, because people reveal what mattered to them about the choice.
Core rules: Offer two mutually exclusive hypothetical options. Everyone chooses and reveals at once, then anyone may explain why. Rotate the question writer; scoring is optional.
Detailed rules: Give the table a moment to think, then vote with one or two fingers. Do not invent a third answer after seeing the votes; passing is fine. For a points game, the writer secretly predicts the majority before the vote and gains one point if correct. A tie earns nothing. Set the turn count in advance.
Recommendation reasons: The vote takes seconds but the reasons can open a much longer conversation. It works both for breaking the ice and for learning how friends think.

Name: Yacht
Conclusion: Your last open box can turn an otherwise excellent roll into a zero.
Core rules: Build dice hands for twelve distinct categories. You get up to three rolls per turn and must fill one unused category each time. Highest total after twelve turns wins.
Detailed rules: Roll five dice and keep or reroll any subset. Ones to sixes count matching faces; Choice takes the full sum. Four of a kind scores the sum of all dice and a full house of exactly three plus two does likewise. The straights 1–5 and 2–6 each score 30, five equal dice score 50. Unmet categories score zero; there is no upper bonus.
Recommendation reasons: The scorecard is short enough to learn quickly, yet deciding whether to save a flexible category for later keeps a straightforward roll interesting.

Name: Yahtzee
Conclusion: A full house on the dice isn't always a full house on your sheet: you might need the points somewhere else.
Core rules: Roll up to three times, keeping any dice you like, then commit the result to one unused score box. After thirteen turns each, the highest total wins.
Detailed rules: Use five dice. Ones through sixes score matching faces; an upper subtotal of 63 earns 35 more. Three and four of a kind score the full sum when qualified; full house scores 25, small straight 30, large straight 40, five of a kind 50 and chance the sum. An impossible category takes zero. This basic scorecard omits repeat-Yahtzee bonuses. Play solo to beat your previous score, or compare totals with any number of opponents.
Recommendation reasons: Five ordinary dice and a score sheet are enough. Whether to bank a safe result or reroll depends on which boxes are still empty, even with the very same dice.
